TOW ARDS EQUIV ARIANT YANG-MILLS THEORY
F. BONECHI, A. S. CATTANEO, AND M. ZABZINE
Abstract. We study four dimensional gauge theories in the con-
text of an equivariant extension of the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV)
formalism. We discuss the embedding of BV Yang-Mills (YM)
theory into a larger BV theory and their relation. Partial inte-
gration in the equivariant BV setting (BV push-forward map) is
performed explicitly for the abelian case. As result, we obtain a
non-local homological generalization of the Cartan calculus and a
non-local extension of the abelian YM BV action which satisﬁes
the equivariant master equation.

1. Introduction
During the last thirty years equivariant localization played an instru-
mental role in the derivation of many exact results in quantum ﬁeld
1

===== PAGE 573 =====
2 F. BONECHI, A. S. CATTANEO, AND M. ZABZINE
theory (QFT), in particular in the context of supersymmetric gaug e
theories. In QFT equivariant localization is based on a clever combi-
nation of the supersymmetry transformations with BRST symmetr y
in such fashion that the resulting transformations are interprete d as
the equivariant diﬀerential on the space of ﬁelds. In our previous w ork
[6] we proposed a framework for the treatment of such theories w ithin
the equivariant extension of the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) formalism.
In the present paper we continue to study this extension and discu ss
the equivariant partial BV integration (equivariant BV push-forwa rd)
map. Our main examples will be four-dimensional gauge theories.
We observe that the BV description of Yang-Mills (YM) theory
given by Costello in [12] can be obtained restricting the BV action
of Donaldson–Witten (DW) theory ([6], [8], [9], [13]) to a BV subman-
ifold. Both theories can be recast in the AKSZ formulation, provided
that, in the case of YM, one allows in the source a diﬀerential graded
algebra (dga) A that is not the external algebra of diﬀerential forms.
The BV push-forward map from DW theory to YM theory corrects t he
Costello’s BV YM action by terms that in the abelian case involve the
zero modes of the ultraviolet (UV) ﬁelds but in the non abelian case
are packed in a full perturbative expansion in the YM ﬁelds. In the
equivariant case, we perform the explicit BV push-forward map in th e
case of abelian theory and obtain an eﬀective action that is non-loca l
and satisﬁes the equivariant master equation. From a geometrical point
of view we can see this result as a non-local homological generalizatio n
of the Cartan calculus.
The paper is organized as follows: in Section 2 we recall basic notions
within the BV formalism and the AKSZ construction of the solution
of the classical master equation. We give the formal deﬁnition of th e
BV push-forward map and list its formal properties. In Section 3 we
summarize the equivariant extension of the BV formalism and the cor -
responding equivariant version of the AKSZ construction. We deﬁn e
formally the equivariant analog of the BV push-forward map and dis-
cuss its properties. In Section 4 we deﬁne the 4d AKSZ theory to
which we refer as the Donaldson–Witten (DW) theory. We discuss
diﬀerent formulations of this theory. In Section 5 we discuss the BV
formulation of Yang–Mills (YM) theory and its relation to the DW
theory. We brieﬂy discuss the application of the BV push-forward m ap
to the abelian DW theory. In Section 6 we introduce the equivariant
extension of DW AKSZ theory. For the case of abelian DW theory we
describe explicitly the equivariant BV push-forward map. The ﬁnal r e-
sult is a non-local deformation of abelian YM theory which satisﬁes th e
equivariant master equation. This provides a non-local Cartan calc ulus

on the dg algebra A. We summarize the paper and discuss the open
questions in 7. Technical details regarding the Hodge decomposition

2.2. AKSZ. The AKSZ formalism [2] is a general procedure to con-
struct solutions of the classical master equation (4) (one checks a pos-
teriori, by restriction to the variables of degree 0 what physical th eory
it describes).
The construction, in d dimensions, requires an odd symplectic man-
ifoldY , with exact symplectic form ωY = dθY of degree d − 1, endowed
with a solution SY (of degree d) of the associated classical master equa-
tion. Given a closed d-manifold Σ d (our space–time), to these data one
associates the odd symplectic manifold M = Map(T [1]Σd,Y ) and a
BV action S satisfying the classical master equation.
We present the construction explictly for Y a ﬁnite-dimensional vec-
tor space and θY = pi dqi. In this case, M has Darboux coordinates
determined by the superﬁelds Pis and Qis, each of which is a sum of
diﬀerential forms on Σ d of all degrees: if a superﬁeld corresponds to
a target variable of degree n, then its k-form component is assigned
degree n −k. The odd symplectic form on M is then deﬁned by

3. Overview of equivariant BV formalisms
3.1. Equivariant BV. In [6] an equivariant version of the BV for-

Remark 6.1. We saw in Section 5.1 that the infrared action SIR,
which is a BV extension of Yang-Mills, is an AKSZ action by itself
with source the dg algebra A deﬁned in (42). It is natural then to look
for the deﬁnition of the Cartan complex for equivariant cohomology
on A and then lifting it to MIR. It is easy to check that while the
Lie derivative Lv ∈ Der(Ω(Σ)[ξ]) descends to Der( A), the same is not
true for ιv ∈ Der(Ω(Σ)[ξ]). So there is not a natural notion for the
contraction operator.

7. Summary
In this paper we considered two four dimensional BV theories: DW
theory associated to BV manifold MDW and YM theory based on BV
manifold MIR (see the text for the deﬁnitions). There exists a formal
push-forward map from MDW to MIR and thus on general ground we
expect that the two theories are quasi-isomorphic at the level of o b-
servables. For example, a local simple observable in one theory can b e
mapped into something complicated and non-local in another theory .
We do not know how much this formal statement is useful for actua l
calculations in one of the theories. In this paper we have performed the
BV push-forward map for the case of abelian theories, and in the ca se
of equivariant theory we obtain non-local corrections to the BV YM
action. The equivariant extension of the BV formalism was originally
introduced in [6] and in this setting upon an appropriate gauge ﬁxing
the residual BRST symmetries should realize the equivariant diﬀeren -
tial on the space of ﬁelds (or some version of equivariant diﬀerentia l).
Such residual BRST symmetries may allow to perform the exact cal-
culations for some theories and for some speciﬁc observables. Thu s we
hope that these new structures presented here can be useful f or the
calculations in the same fashion as the equivariant considerations he lp
calculate the ordinary integrals of the closed diﬀerential forms. Bu t
this requires further study.
Another interesting result of this work is the homological general-
ization of Cartan calculus with the explicit constructions in terms of
non-local operators. This structure requires further study an d better
understanding both at the level of the formal properties and at t he
level of concrete examples. It would be interesting to see if any of t he

===== PAGE 596 =====
TOW ARDS EQUIV ARIANT YANG-MILLS THEORY 25
standard considerations for the equivariant cohomology and equiv ari-
ant localization can be generalized to this new setting.

FRACTIONAL HARDY INEQUALITIES AND CAPACITY DENSITY
LIZAVETA IHNATSYEVA, KAUSHIK MOHANTA, AND ANTTI V. V¨AH¨AKANGAS
Abstract. We prove that a pointwise fractional Hardy inequality implies a fractional Hardy
inequality, deﬁned via a Gagliardo-type seminorm. The proof consist s of two main parts. The
ﬁrst one is to characterize the pointwise fractional Hardy inequalit y in terms of a fractional
capacity density condition. The second part is to show the deep ope n-endedness or self-
improvement property of the fractional capacity density, which w e accomplish in the setting
of a complete geodesic space equipped with a doubling measure. These results are new already
in the standard Euclidean setting.
1. Introduction
This paper brings together the pointwise fractional Hardy inequalities introduced in [10] and
the recent developments on self-improvement of nonlocal capacit y density conditions from
[39, 7, 6, 36]. The motivation for our nonlocal problems comes from their local an alogues.
Recall that a closed set E in a metric measure space, equipped with a doubling measure,
supports a pointwise p-Hardy inequality if there exists a constant CH such that inequality
|u(x)| ≤ CH dist(x,E )(M2 dist(x,E)(gp)(x))1/p (1)

in [ 32] that a pointwise p-Hardy inequality is equivalent to the so-called p-capacity density
condition of E. By using this equivalence and the deep result on the self-improveme nt of
the p-capacity density condition, see below, it was shown in [ 32] that the pointwise p-Hardy
inequality (1) implies the integral Hardy inequality

The key fact above is the self-improvement, meaning that a p-capacity density condition
implies an a priori stronger ˆp-capacity density condition, for some 1 < ˆp<p . The p-capacity
density condition, also known as uniform p-fatness, appears in Hardy inequalities, potential
theory and PDE’s, we refer to [ 25, 30]. The self-improvement property of this condition was
ﬁrst discovered by Lewis [ 39] using potential theory in Euclidean spaces. His result has been
followed by other works incorporating diﬀerent techniques, such a s nonlinear potential theory
[43, 5] and Hardy inequalities [ 33, 37]. A direct proof for the self-improvement of pointwise
Hardy inequalities by using curves is given in [15, 14]. For a survey on Hardy inequalities, and
their connections to the p-capacity density condition, we refer to [ 29, 12, 30].
Our main contribution is an extension of the approach and results in [ 32] to the nonlocal
setting of fractional Sobolev spaces and their generalizations. So me of the ﬁrst steps were

FRACTIONAL HARDY INEQUALITIES AND CAPACITY DENSITY 3
A more speciﬁc outline for the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the standing
assumptions and notation, and recall some concepts that are nee ded later on. For instance,
the fractional Poincar´ e inequalities are recalled from [10]. An important notion of a fractional
relative capacity is deﬁned in Section 3, where we also give estimates for relative capacities of
balls and lower bounds for relative capacities of closed sets in terms of Hausdorﬀ contents. The
fractional (β,p,q )-capacity density condition is introduced in Section 4, where its equivalence
with the pointwise (β,p,q )-Hardy inequality (3) is also shown. In Section 5 we deﬁne certain
Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin seminorms and we show in Section6 that these seminorms are often
comparable to Gagliardo-type seminorms that are used to deﬁne th e fractional capacities. A
Sobolev–Poincar´ e type inequality is a key tool here, see Lemma 5.3. The comparability of
fractional and Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin relative capacities followsfrom the equivalence of the
corresponding seminorms, as it is shown in Section 7. Using the capacity comparison and
results from [ 36], we obtain a q-independence property for the fractional relative capacity in
Theorem 7.6; we refer to [2, Sections 3.6 and 4.4] for analogous properties of Triebel–Lizorkin
capacities in Euclidean spaces. Using the capacity comparison result s from Section 7 and [36,
Theorem 11.4], in Section 8 we show that the fractional ( β,p,q )-capacity density condition
has three ways of self-improvement, with respect to parameters β, p and q, see Theorem 8.5.
Our main results are proved in the last Section 9, including Theorem 9.3 that follows from
the self-improvement of the pointwise Hardy inequality in Theorem 9.2.
Finally, we make some remarks on the line of research developed in [ 39], [7], [6], [36]. The
origins of our results can be traced to the seminal work by Lewis [ 39], who proved that a
Riesz (β,p )-capacity density condition in Euclidean spaces is doubly self-improv ing, that is,
self-improving in both parameters β and p. More recently, a Haj/suppress lasz (β,p )-capacity density
condition in metric spaces was introduced in [7] by using Haj/suppress lasz gradients of order 0<β ≤ 1.
It was also shown that this condition is doubly self-improving, if X is a complete geodesic
space. The comparability of Riesz and Haj/suppress lasz (β,p )-capacities was shown in [6], where Lewis’
result was also transferred to complete geodesic spaces. A ﬂexible and a priori more general
Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin (β,p,q )-capacity density condition was introduced in [ 36] by using
fractional Haj/suppress lasz gradients and Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin seminorms, see Deﬁnition 8.1. The
Riesz (β,p )-capacity density condition for 0 < β < 1 is its special case, corresponding to
the indices (β,p, ∞). It was shown in [ 36] that the Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin (β,p,q )-capacity
density condition is self-improving in all three parameters β, p, q and, in fact, independent
of the q-parameter, under suitable assumptions. Consequently, the a priori strongest Riesz
(β,p )-capacity density condition is equivalent to a Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin (β,p,q )-capacity
density condition, for all 1 <q ≤ ∞. Theorems 7.6 and 8.5 complement this line of research,
the former proving the q-independence of the fractional capacity, and the latter proving the
self-improvement of a fractional capacity density condition in all th ree parameters.

2. Preliminaries
Throughout the paper we assume that X = (X,d,µ ) is a metric measure space equipped
with a metric d and a nonnegative complete Borel measure µ such that 0 <µ (B)< ∞ for all

choose n0 be the smallest integer such that 2 −n0 ≤ 2 diam(X). In the latter case, we have
diam(X)< 2−n0 ≤ 2 diam(X).

4. Fractional capacity density condition
In this section, we ﬁrst deﬁne the fractional capacity density con dition, see Deﬁnition 4.1.
We also deﬁne the boundary Poincar´ e and pointwise Hardy inequalities in Deﬁnition 4.2. The
counterparts of Deﬁnitions 4.1 and 4.2 in the local case of upper gradients can be found in [32].
We prove three Lemmata 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5, whose combination gives rise to a characterization
of the fractional capacity density condition in terms of a boundary Poincar´ e and a pointwise
Hardy inequality, we refer to Theorem 4.6.
Motivated by [10] and [36], we deﬁne the fractional capacity density condition as follows.
Deﬁnition 4.1. Let 1 ≤ p,q < ∞, 0 < β <1, and let E ⊂ X be a closed set. We say that
E satisﬁes the fractional (β,p,q )-capacity density condition if there are constants c0 > 0 and
Λ> 2 such that

for all x ∈E and all 0 <r< (1/8) diam(E).

Poincar´ e inequalities and pointwise Hardy inequalities are deﬁned as follows, as in [ 10].

The following theorem characterizes the fractional capacity dens ity condition in connected
metric spaces. This result is a nonlocal or fractional analogue of [ 32, Theorem 2]. To our
knowledge, Theorem 4.6 is new in this generality.
Theorem 4.6. Let 1 ≤p< ∞, 1 ≤q <∞ and 0<β < 1. Assume that X is connected. Let
E ⊂X be a closed set. Then the following conditions are equivalen t:
(i) E satisﬁes the fractional (β,p,q )-capacity density condition (19).
(ii) E supports the boundary (β,p,p,q )-Poincar´ e inequality(20).
(iii) E supports the pointwise (β,p,q )-Hardy inequality (21).
Proof. Since the metric space X is connected, the measure µ satisﬁes the quantitative reverse
doubling condition ( 10), with constants σ > 0 and cσ > 0. By Lemma 2.5, we see that X
supports the ( β,p,p,q )-Poincar´ e inequality. Hence, the implication (i) to (ii) follows from
Lemma 4.3. Lemma 4.4 shows that (ii) implies (iii). The last implication from (iii) to (i)
follows from Lemma 4.5. □

===== PAGE 612 =====
14 L. IHNATSYEV A, K. MOHANTA, AND A. V. V ¨AH ¨AKANGAS
Remark 4.7. Suppose that a closed setE ⊂X supports the pointwise (β,p,q )-Hardy inequal-
ity (21), for some 1 ≤p,q < ∞ and 0 < β <1. From Deﬁnition 4.2(ii), it easily follows that
E supports the pointwise ( ˆβ, ˆp,q )-Hardy inequality if p ≤ ˆp< ∞ and β ≤ ˆβ <1. In the light
of Theorem 4.6, a corresponding monotonicity result holds for the fractional cap acity density
condition in connected metric spaces, as well as for the boundary P oincar´ e inequality. Under
certain restrictions, the third parameter q can be decreased, using Theorem 7.4. Our main
result, Theorem 8.5, gives nontrivial extensions of the above mentioned three monoto nicity
properties in complete geodesic spaces.
Remark 4.8. The connectivity of the spaceX is assumed in many results during this section.
By examining the proofs, one could replace this assumption by requiring that, for all 0<κ< 1,
there exists 0 <c R < 1 such that inequality ( 9) holds. This holds in connected metric spaces
by [4, Lemma 3.7]. We omit the corresponding slightly more general formula tions.
5. Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin seminorms
One of our main goals is to show a self-improvement property for the fractional capacity
density condition ( 19), see Theorem 8.4. In order to show this result, we make use of a self-
improvement property of a closely related Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel-Lizorkin capacity density condition,
which was recently established in [ 36]. Our basic strategy of proof is to show that these two
capacity density conditions are equivalent under certain assumptio ns. For this purpose, we
ﬁrst recall local variants of Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin seminorms inthis section. Later we need
a Sobolev–Poincar´ e type inequality in Lemma5.3. Its proof is recalled for convenience.
First we deﬁne fractional Haj/suppress lasz gradients in open sets as in [22], by adapting the global
deﬁnition in [34].
Deﬁnition 5.1. Let 0 < β <1 and let u: Ω → R be a measurable function on an open set
Ω ⊂ X. A sequence g = (gk)k∈Z of nonnegative measurable functions is called a fractional
β-Haj/suppress lasz gradient ofu in Ω if there exists a set E ⊂ Ω such that µ(E) = 0 and for all k ∈ Z
and x,y ∈ Ω \E satisfying 2 −k−1 ≤d(x,y )< 2−k, we have
|u(x) −u(y)| ≤ d(x,y )β(gk(x) +gk(y)).

7. Comparison of relative capacities
In this section, we ﬁrst deﬁne a relative Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin capacity by following
[36], see Deﬁnition 7.1. The seminorm comparison in Section 6 immediately yields a two-sided
comparison between the relative fractional and Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin capacities, we refer to
Theorem 7.3. As an application, we obtain a q-monotonicity property of fractional capacities,
see the second inequality in ( 42) and Theorem 7.4. Under more restrictive assumptions, we
also establish a deeperq-independence property of fractional capacities, see Theorem 7.6. This
follows, via comparison of capacities, from the corresponding q-independence results in [ 36]
for relative Haj/suppress lasz–Triebel–Lizorkin capacities.

8. Three ways of self-improvement
In this section we prove one of our main result, Theorem 8.5. This result gives three ways
of self-improvement for the fractional capacity density condition in a complete geodesic space:
with respect to the parametersβ,p andq. That is, if a closed setE ⊂X satisﬁes the fractional
(β,p,q )-capacity density condition ( 19) with suitable restrictions on β, p and q, then there
exists ε> 0 such that E satisﬁes the fractional ( ˆβ, ˆp, ˆq)-capacity density condition (19), if
|β − ˆβ|<ε, |p − ˆp|<ε and 1 ≤ ˆq <∞.

the capacity comparison in Section 7. The basic estimates in Section 3 are also useful here.

The following corollary explicates a three way self-improvement prop erty of the fractional
capacity density condition in complete geodesic spaces, under suita ble restrictions on the
parameters, most notable of which are the inequalities Q(1/p − 1/q)<β <σ/p .
Theorem 8.5. Let (X,d,µ ) be a complete geodesic space equipped with a doubling measur e µ
which satisﬁes the quantitative doubling condition (8), with exponent Q >0, and the quanti-
tative reverse doubling condition (10), with exponent σ >0. Let 1<p,q < ∞ and 0<β < 1
be such that Q(1/p − 1/q)<β <σ/p . Assume that a closed set E ⊂X satisﬁes the fractional
(β,p,q )-capacity density condition (19). Then there exists ε> 0 such that E satisﬁes also the
fractional ( ˆβ, ˆp, ˆq)-capacity density condition (19), if
|β − ˆβ|<ε, |p − ˆp|<ε and 1 ≤ ˆq <∞. (56)
Proof. Theorem 8.4 shows that E satisﬁes the Hausdorﬀ content density condition ( 47) for
some 0 < d < βp. Choose ε >0 such that the following inequalities 1 < ˆp <∞, 0 < ˆβ <1,
and 0 < d <ˆβ ˆp hold for all ˆβ, ˆp satisfying the ( 56). This is clearly possible, since all of the
three inequalities are open-ended and the parameters β and p satisfy them.
Now, assume that ( 56) holds for the chosen ε >0. In particular, E satisﬁes the Hausdorﬀ
content density condition ( 47) for 0 < d <ˆβˆp. Since X is connected, the measure µ satisﬁes
the reverse doubling condition (9), with constantsκ = 1/2 and 0<c R =C(cµ)< 1. The other
assumptions of Theorem 8.3 are also satisﬁed, with parameters ˆβ, ˆp and ˆq, and the theorem
implies that E satisﬁes the fractional ( ˆβ, ˆp, ˆq)-capacity density condition (19). □
9. Fractional Hardy inequalities
A combination of Theorems 8.5 and 4.6 provides three ways of self-improvement for a
pointwise Hardy inequality in complete geodesic spaces, in terms of β, p and q satisfying
suitable restrictions. Here we make use of this result and show that a pointwise (β,p,q )-
Hardy inequality implies the following variant of the integral ( β,p,q )-Hardy inequality.

OLLIVIER-RICCI CUR V A TURE OF REGULAR GRAPHS
MORITZ HEHL
Abstract. We derive explicit formulas for the Lin-Lu-Yau curvature an d the α-Ollivier-
Ricci curvature in terms of graph parameters and an optimal a ssignment. Utilizing these
precise expressions, we examine the relationship between t he Lin-Lu-Yau curvature κ and
the 0-Ollivier-Ricci curvature κ0, resulting in an equality condition on regular graphs.
This condition allows us to characterize edges that are bone idle in regular graphs of
girth four and to construct a family of bone idle graphs with t his girth. We then use
our formulas to provide an eﬃcient implementation of the Oll ivier-Ricci curvature on
regular graphs, enabling us to identify all bone idle, regul ar graphs with fewer than 15
vertices. Moreover, we establish a rigidity theorem for coc ktail party graphs, proving
that a regular graph is a cocktail party graph if and only if it s Lin-Lu-Yau curvature is
equal to one. Furthermore, we present a condition on the degr ee of a regular graph that
guarantees positive Ricci curvature. We conclude this work by discussing the maximal
number of vertices that a d-regular graph with positive Lin-Lu-Yau curvature can have .

1. Introduction
Since F. Gauss and B. Riemann introduced the geometric notio n of curvature over 150
years ago, it played a central role in diﬀerential geometry. T he curvature of a space refers
to the degree to which it deviates from being ﬂat. Ricci curva ture is one of the various
notions that are of importance. It is a fundamental concept i n diﬀerential geometry,
particularly in the study of Riemannian manifolds. Broadly speaking, Ricci curvature
measures the extent to which the geometry of a Riemannian man ifold deviates locally
from that of a Euclidean space. It plays a crucial role in vari ous areas of mathematics
and theoretical physics. In the general theory of relativit y, it appears in Einstein’s ﬁeld
equations, where the Ricci curvature tensor is part of the Ei nstein tensor, which describes
the curvature of spacetime. It is also a crucial ingredient f or the Ricci ﬂow, introduced in
Richard Hamilton’s groundbreaking work from 1982 [17]. Rec ently, the Ricci ﬂow has led
to the proof of the Poincar´ e conjecture and the more general Geometrization conjecture.
Gromov’s work [16] demonstrates the important role of the Ri cci curvature tensor in
Riemannian geometry.
Given the importance of Ricci curvature in diﬀerential geome try, there is a clear interest
in extending this concept to metric spaces more general than Riemannian manifolds. This
motivation has led to the proposal of various generalized no tions of curvature for non-
smooth or discrete structures. This contrasts with Riemann ian geometry, where we have
a unique notion of Ricci curvature. Every approach captures a diﬀerent aspect of the
Riemannian notion, and each is thus suited for a diﬀerent purp ose.
In their 1985 paper [1], Bakry and ´Emery proposed a generalized notion within the broad
framework of a Markov semigroup, the Bakry- ´Emery curvature . It is motivated by the
curvature dimension inequality and the Bakry-´Emery Γ calculus. The Bakry-´Emery theory
applied to graphs has received considerable interest (see, e.g., [23] and [24]).
Another approach, taken by Erbar and Maas [13] and by Mielke [ 30], uses the convexity
of the entropy to introduce a discrete Ricci curvature notio n.
Forman’s work [15], introduces a discretization of the classical Ricci curvature on CW com-
plexes, the Forman-Ricci curvature. This deﬁnition is based on the Bochner-Weitzenb¨ ock
formula. Sreejith et al. [42] adapted Forman’s notion to the case of graphs.
The Forman-Ricci curvature is highly correlated [38] with, and in certain cases even co-
incides [18] with, the curvature notion we consider in this w ork, the Ollivier-Ricci curva-
ture. In 2009, Ollivier [36] developed this discrete Ricci curva ture notion on metric spaces
equipped with Markov chains or with a measure.

Figure 1. Positive vs. negative sectional curvature.
In the work by von Renesse and Sturm [37], it was shown that Riemannian manifolds with
positive Ricci curvature are characterized by the property that small spheres are closer to
one another than their centers are. Namely, let M be a Riemannian manifold. Consider a
tangent vectorω = (xy). Let νx be another tangent vector at x and let νy be the tangent
vector at y obtained by parallel transport of νx along ω from x to y. If the geodesic
starting at x in direction νx and the geodesic starting at y in direction νy converge, then
the sectional curvature is positive. If the geodesics are pa rallel, then sectional curvature
is zero and if they diverge it is negative. The Ricci curvatur e at ω = (xy) is obtained by
averaging over all directions νx at x. Now, a point on a small sphere Sx around x can be
thought of as a direction νx. Thus, on average, Ricci curvature determines if a point on
Sx and the corresponding point on Sy are closer than x and y or further away. Figure 1
[36] illustrates this key observation.
With this characterization in mind, we now turn to Ollivier’ s generalization to the frame-
work of metric spaces. Instead of the sphere Sx centered at a point x, Ollivier uses
probability measures mx supported in the neighborhood of x. More precisely, let ( X,d )
be a Polish metric space, equipped with its Borel σ-algebra. A family of probability mea-
suresm ={mx :x∈X} is called a random walk m onX if the two technical assumptions
are satisﬁed [36]:
(i) The measure mx depends measurably on x∈X.
(ii) Each measure mx has ﬁnite ﬁrst moment, i.e., for some (hence any) z ∈ X and
for any x ∈X:
∫
d(z,y )dmx(y)<∞.
As an analogue for the average distance between correspondi ng points on Sx and Sy,
Ollivier uses the Wasserstein distance W1 between the probability measures mx and my.
Thus, optimal transport theory is an essential ingredient f or this notion of discrete Ricci
curvature. In what follows, we introduce some basic concept s of the optimal transport
theory and refer the interested reader to the very comprehen sive book by Villani [43].
Following the case of Riemannian manifolds, the comparison of the distance ofmx andmy
with the distance ofx andy determines the sign of the Ollivier Ricci curvature. Namely, in
the case that the probability measuresmx andmy are closer thanx andy, Ricci curvature
will be positive, otherwise negative. This leads to the foll owing deﬁnition.
Deﬁnition 1.1 (Ollivier-Ricci curvature, [36]) . Let (X,d ) be a metric space with a col-
lection of probability measures m ={mx :x∈X}. For two distinct points x,y ∈X, the
3

Ollivier-Ricci curvature of (X,d,m ) along (x,y ) is deﬁned as
κ(x,y ) = 1− W1(mx,my)
d(x,y ) .
Rather than thinking of mx as an analogue for the sphere centered at x, Ollivier proposes
another, more probabilistic, way to think about it. That is, as deﬁning a Markov chain
with n-step transition probability from x to y given by:

In [36], Ollivier shows that up to some scaling factor, this deﬁnition captures the Riemann-
ian Ricci curvature in the case of a Riemannian manifold equi pped with the Riemannian
volume measure. This reﬁnes Theorem 1.5 in the paper by von Re nesse and Sturm [37].
The Ollivier-Ricci curvature in the context of locally ﬁnit e graphs has recently garnered
signiﬁcant attention. This has led to numerous compelling t heoretical results, extending
various classical theorems from Riemannian geometry to the graph setting. These include
spectral gap estimates, concentration of measure, and log- Sobolev inequalities [35].
On the other hand, this discrete curvature notion was found to be beneﬁcial in the analysis
of complex networks. In the realm of network science, graph c urvature holds general
interest because numerous real-world networks exhibit various forms of geometry [4]. The
Ollivier-Ricci curvature can oﬀer valuable insights into th e geometry of these networks.
It has recently found applications in numerous practical co ntexts, e.g., in the analysis of
the internet topology [34], as an economic indicator for mar ket fragility and systemic risk
[40], to diﬀerentiate cancer networks [39] or in the study of b rain structural networks [14].
Furthermore, Ollivier-Ricci curvature ﬁnds applications in machine learning. In [33] and
[41], the authors propose Ollivier-Ricci curvature based a pproaches to community detec-
tion. Regarding graph neural networks (GNNs), Ollivier-Ri cci curvature provides a uni-
ﬁed framework for studying over-squashing and over-smoothing, two inherent problems of
these models [32]. Recently, new GNN architectures, incorp orating graph curvature, were
proposed [44, 20]. These curvature-based graph neural netw orks (CGNNs) outperform
state-of-the-art methods on various synthetic and real-wo rld networks.
On graphs, Ollivier’s notion of Ricci curvature κα takes values on edges and depends on
an idleness parameterα∈ [0, 1]. Ollivier considered idleness parameters α = 0 andα = 1
2.
In 2011, Lin, Lu, and Yau [22] introduced a modiﬁcation of the Ollivier-Ricci curvature,
by computing the derivative of the curvature with respect to the idleness parameter. We
will refer to this modiﬁcation as Lin-Lu-Yau curvature . The relationship between the
Lin-Lu-Yau curvature and the original α-Ollivier-Ricci curvature was studied by Bourne
et al. in [6]. One of the main contributions of this work will b e to provide answers to
open questions proposed in this paper. Namely, we will give a necessary and suﬃcient
condition on regular graphs for κ0(x,y ) =κ(x,y ). Using this, we will provide a necessary
and suﬃcient condition for an edge to be bone idle on a graph of girth four. That means
κα(x,y ) = 0 for any α∈ [0, 1]. We furthermore construct an inﬁnite family of bone idle,
regular graphs with a girth of four. Moreover, we prove thatκ(x,y )> 0 implies on regular
graphs that κ0(x,y )≥ 0 and we construct non-regular graphs with edges x∼y satisfying
κ(x,y )> 0 and κ0(x,y )< 0.
To this end, we derive explicit Ricci curvature formulas for regular graphs. Bonini et al.
[5, Theorem 4.6] derive an exact formula for the Lin-Lu-Yau curvature on strongly regular
4

===== PAGE 632 =====
graphs in terms of graph parameters and the size of a maximal matching in the core neigh-
borhood. M¨ unch et al. [31, Theorem 2.6] show an exact formula for a modiﬁed curvature
notion on combinatorial graphs. There is an overlap between some of our methods and
theirs.
To my knowledge, precise expressions for the Lin-Lu-Yau cur vature and the α-Ollivier-
Ricci curvature on arbitrary regular graphs have not yet bee n established. Using these
precise expressions, we provide an eﬃcient implementation for the Ollivier-Ricci curvature
on regular graphs. Additionally, we use these results to est ablish a rigidity theorem for
cocktail party graphs and to give a condition on the degree ofa regular graph, guaranteeing
that it is of positive Ricci curvature.
1.1. Outline. In Chapter 2, we introduce the necessary concepts of graph th eory and
optimal transport theory. In Chapter 3, the Ollivier-Ricci curvature on graphs, as well
as the modiﬁcation by Lin, Lu, and Yau, will be presented. In C hapter 4, we derive our
precise expressions for the diﬀerent curvature notions. Cha pter 5 is devoted to the study
of the relationship between the Lin-Lu-Yau curvatureκ and the 0-Ollivier-Ricci curvature
κ0. In Chapter 6, we present the implementation of the Ollivier-Ricci curvature on regular
graphs and the results obtained by applying it to exhaustive lists of regular graphs with
a given number of vertices and degree.
2. Preliminaries
We begin by reviewing some fundamental concepts of graph theory and optimal transport
theory. Those seeking a thorough introduction to these area s are encouraged to consult
the works of Diestel [11] for graph theory and Villani [43] fo r optimal transport theory.
2.1. Graph theory. A simple graph G = (V,E ) is an unweighted, undirected graph that
contains no multiple edges or self-loops. We call V the vertex set andE the edge set. For
two verticesx,y∈V we denote the existence of an edge between x and y byx∼y.
Denote byd(x,y ) the shortest path distance betweenx andy, i.e., the number of edges in
a shortest path connecting them. If no such path exists, d(x,y ) is deﬁned to be inﬁnity.
For two nonempty sets A,B⊂V , we deﬁne
dist(A,B ) = inf{d(x,y ) :x∈A,y∈B}.
The diameter of a graph G is deﬁned as the length of the longest shortest path, that is,
diam(G) = max
x,y∈V
d(x,y ).
The girth of a graph is the length of a shortest cycle contained in the gr aph. The girth is
deﬁned to be inﬁnity if the graph does not contain any cycles.
Givenx∈V , deﬁne
Sr(x) :={y∈V :d(x,y ) =r}, B r(x) :={y∈V :d(x,y )≤r}.
For an edgex∼y, we denote by△(x,y ) the set of common neighbors of x andy, that is,
△(x,y ) =S1(x)∩S1(y).
Denote by dx the degree of x, that is, dx =|S1(x)|. The graph G is called locally ﬁnite if
every vertex has ﬁnite degree. The graph G is said to be d-regular if every vertex has the
same degree d.

A d-regular graph G with n vertices is called strongly regular with parameters (n,d,λ,µ )
if every two adjacent vertices have λ≥ 0 common neighbors and every two nonadjacent
vertices haveµ≥ 1 common neighbors.
We end this section by introducing another important class o f graphs. A simple graph
G = (V,E ) is called bipartite, if there is a partition ofV into two disjoint subsetsV =A∪B,
such that every edge connects a vertex in A to a vertex in B. If the partition V =A∪B
is speciﬁed, we denote the bipartite graph by G = (A,B,E ).
In what follows,G = (V,E ) is always assumed to be a locally ﬁnite, connected and simpl e
graph.

measures on V . We now introduce a metric on P(V ), the 1-Wasserstein distance.

The following Lemma, which is intuitively clear, allows us t o impose some assumptions
on an optimal transport plan. It states that it is not necessa ry to move any mass that is
shared between the probability measures.
Lemma 2.1. LetG = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph and let µ1,µ 2 be two probability mea-
sures on V. Then there exists an optimal transport plan π transportingµ1 to µ2 satisfying
π(x,x ) = min{µ1(x),µ 2(x)}

[6, Lemma 4.1].
The Kantorovich duality is a fundamental concept in optimal transport theory (see The-
orem 1.3 in [43]). Here, we introduce it in our speciﬁc graph s etting. For that, we deﬁne
the notion of 1-Lipschitz functions.
Deﬁnition 2.2 (1-Lipschitz function). LetG = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. A function
f :V→ R is called 1-Lipschitz if
|f(x)−f(y)|≤ d(x,y ), ∀x,y∈V.
The set of all 1-Lipschitz functions on V is denoted by 1-Lip.

In this chapter, we shall introduce Ollivier’s discrete not ion of Ricci curvature on graphs,
as well as the modiﬁcation introduced by Lin, Lu, and Yau.

We write Ric(G)≥ k if κ(x,y )≥k for all x,y ∈V . The subsequent Lemma states that
provingκ(x,y )≥k for adjacent vertices x∼y is suﬃcient to show that Ric(G)≥k.
Lemma 3.1 ([22], Lemma 2.3) . Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. If κ(x,y )≥ k
for any edge (x,y )∈E, then κ(x,y )≥k for any two vertices x,y∈V .
Therefore, in what follows, we will only consider κ(x,y ) for adjacent vertices x∼y. We
write Ric(G) =k if κ(x,y ) =k for all edges x∼y.

3.3. The core neighborhood. For two adjacent verticesx∼y, the Ollivier-Ricci curva-

vertices with a distance less than or equal to two from x and y are relevant for the opti-
mal transport problem. Therefore, the Wasserstein distanc e, and hence the Ollivier-Ricci
curvature, is a local property. We deﬁne the core neighborhood of an edge x∼y as
Nxy =S1(x)∪S1(y)∪Pxy,
where Pxy ={i∈ V : d(x,i ) = d(y,i ) = 2}. According to the above reasoning, the
Ollivier-Ricci curvature should only depend on the core nei ghborhood of an edge. The
following Lemma makes this statement precise.

4. Exact expressions of Ollivier-Ricci curvature
The aim of this chapter is to derive precise expressions of th e Lin-Lu-Yau curvature and
the α-Ollivier-Ricci curvature of an edge x∼ y with dx = dy. These expressions are
formulated in terms of the graph parameters and an optimal as signment of vertices in the
core neighborhood.
Bourne et al. [6] showed that the idleness function α↦→κα(x,y ) is piecewise linear. If
x and y are of equal degree d, κα(x,y ) has at most two linear parts. More precisely, the
idleness function is linear on the intervals [0, 1/(d + 1)] and [1/(d + 1), 1]. We will provide
exact formulas for κα on the two linear parts.
4.1. Decomposing the neighborhood. In the previous chapter, we have already seen
that the Ricci-curvature is a local property dependent sole ly on the core neighborhood of
an edge.
In what follows, we will see that the Ricci curvature of an edg e x∼ y with dx = dy can
be further simpliﬁed. To this end, we decompose the 1-step ne ighborhood of the vertices
x and y into disjoint sets. We denote by △(x,y ) the set of common neighbors of both x
and y, namely,
△(x,y ) =S1(x)∩S1(y).
Thus,|△(x,y )| is the number of 3-cycles in G supported on the edge x∼y.
Furthermore, we deﬁne
Rx(x,y ) =S1(x)\ (△(x,y )∪{y}) and Ry(x,y ) =S1(y)\ (△(x,y )∪{x}),
giving rise to the following disjoint decompositions of S1(x) and S1(y).
S1(x) ={y}∪△ (x,y )∪Rx(x,y ) and S1(y) ={x}∪△ (x,y )∪Ry(x,y ).
Using these decompositions, we argue that the computation o f the 1-Wasserstein distance
reduces to an assignment problem betweenRx(x,y ) andRy(x,y ). Therefore, we introduce
the concept of optimal assignments.
Deﬁnition 4.1 (Optimal assignment) . Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. Let
U,W ⊂V with|U| =|W|<∞. We call a bijection φ :U→W an assignment betweenU
and W . Denote by AUW the set of all assignments between U and W . We call φ∈A UW
an optimal assignment betweenU and W if

Remark. Observe that forU =W =∅,AUW contains the empty function. Hence,AUW ⁄=
∅ andOUW ⁄=∅ always holds true.

Deﬁnition 4.2 (Perfect matching). Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. A perfect
matching between two disjoint subsets U,W ⊂ V is a bijective map φ : U → W , with
d(z,φ (z)) = 1 for all z∈U.
Note that for an edge x∼ y with dx = dy, we have|Rx(x,y )| =|Ry(x,y )|. For the sake
of simplicity, we will denote by Axy andOxy the setsARx(x,y)Ry(x,y) andORx(x,y)Ry(x,y),
respectively.
For an assignment φ∈A xy, we associate the following sets:
• □(φ): The neighbors of x, forming a 4-cycle based at the edge x∼ y, with their
image under φ. That is, □(φ) ={z∈Rx(x,y ) :d(z,φ (z)) = 1}.
• (φ): The neighbors of x, forming a 5-cycle based at the edge x∼ y, with their
image under φ. That is, (φ) ={z∈Rx(x,y ) :d(z,φ (z)) = 2}.

4.4. Strongly regular graphs. Bonini et al. [5] derive an exact formula for the Lin-Lu-
Yau curvature on strongly regular graphs. In this section, w e show that our formula for
arbitrary regular graphs reduces to the formula provided by Bonini et al. in the case of
strongly regular graphs.
First, we recall the deﬁnition of a strongly regular graph.
Deﬁnition 4.3 (Strongly regular graph) . A d-regular graph G = (V,E ) with n vertices
is said to be strongly regular with parameters (n,d,λ,µ ), if every two adjacent vertices
have λ≥ 0 common neighbors and every two nonadjacent vertices have µ≥ 1 common
neighbors.
Note that the diameter of a strongly regular graph is less tha n or equal to two. In
particular, every node i ∈ Rx(x,y ) is at a distance less than or equal to two from a
node j∈ Rx(x,y ). Using this property, we obtain the following precise form ula for the
Lin-Lu-Yau curvature on strongly regular graphs.

5.3. Bone idleness. We introduce the notion of bone idle, initially proposed by B ourne
et al. in [6].
Deﬁnition 5.1 (Bone idle) . Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. We say an edge
x∼y is bone idle if κα(x,y ) = 0 for every α∈ [0, 1]. We say that G is bone idle if every
edge is bone idle.
25

===== PAGE 653 =====
The notion of Ricci-ﬂatness is weaker but strongly related t o bone idleness.
Deﬁnition 5.2 (Ricci-ﬂat). LetG = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. We call G Ricci-ﬂat
if κ(x,y ) = 0 for every edge. We call G α-Ricci-ﬂat if κα(x,y ) = 0 for every edge.
Lemma 5.6. LetG = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph. Let x,y∈V with x∼y. Then the
following are equivalent:
(i) κα(x,y ) = 0 for all α∈ [0, 1].
(ii) κ0(x,y ) =κ(x,y ) = 0.
Proof. (ii) =⇒ (i). Let α∈ (0, 1) be arbitrary. Assume κ0(x,y ) = κ(x,y ) = 0. Recall
that the idleness function is concave, and also note that κ1(x,y ) = 0. Hence,
κα(x,y )≥ακ1(x,y ) + (1−α)κ0(x,y ) = 0.
The other inequality follows from the fact that the graph of a concave function lies below
its tangent line at each point and that κ′
1 =−κ:
κα(x,y )≤κ1(x,y ) +κ′
1(x,y )· (α− 1) =κ(x,y )· (1−α) = 0.
(i) =⇒ (ii). This is an immediate consequence of the deﬁnition of κ. □
Therefore, a graph is bone idle if it is Ricci-ﬂat and 0-Ricci -ﬂat. Previous works have
addressed the classiﬁcation of Ricci-ﬂat graphs. Bhattach arya et al. [3] classiﬁed all
graphs that are 0-Ricci-ﬂat and have girth at least ﬁve.
Theorem 5.7 ([3], Corollary 4.1) . Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph with girth at
least ﬁve. Suppose that G is 0-Ricci-ﬂat. Then G is isomorphic to one of the following
graphs:
(i) The inﬁnite path,
(ii) the inﬁnite ray,
(iii) the path Pn for n≥ 2,
(iv) the cycle graph Cn for n≥ 5,
(v) the star graph Tn for n≥ 3.
On the other hand, Cushing et al. classiﬁed all Ricci-ﬂat gra phs with girth at least ﬁve
[9].
Theorem 5.8 ([9], Theorem 1). LetG = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph with girth at least
ﬁve. Suppose that G is Ricci-ﬂat. Then G is isomorphic to one of the following graphs:
(i) The inﬁnite path,
(ii) the cycle graph Cn for n≥ 6,
(iii) the dodecahedral graph,
(iv) the Petersen graph,
(v) the half-dodecahedral graph,
(vi) the Triplex graph.
Combining Theorem 5.7 and Theorem 5.8 yields the following result:
Corollary 5.9. Let G = (V,E ) be a locally ﬁnite graph with girth at least ﬁve. Suppose
that G is bone idle. Then G is isomorphic to one of the following graphs:
(i) The inﬁnite path,
(ii) the cycle graph Cn for n≥ 6.

6. Implementation
In this chapter, we introduce an eﬃcient implementation of t he Ollivier-Ricci curvature
on regular graphs. Additionally, we explore an interesting problem in graph theory: the
enumeration of all regular graphs up to isomorphism. Leveraging these ﬁndings, we classify
all regular, bone idle graphs with a small number of vertices and establish a rigidity
theorem for cocktail party graphs. Finally, we present a con dition that ensures a regular
graph G satisﬁes Ric(G)> 0.
6.1. Linear assignment problem. As demonstrated in preceding chapters, the compu-
tation of the Ollivier-Ricci curvature on regular graphs simpliﬁes to identifying an optimal
assignment between two distinct sets of vertices of equal ca rdinality, denoted by n.
This problem referred to as the linear assignment problem , stands as a fundamental task
in linear optimization. With a rich history dating back to th e early 20th century, the
linear assignment problem has garnered signiﬁcant attenti on in the literature. Thereby
leading to the development of eﬃcient algorithms for its solution. The earliest algorithms,
proposed in the 1940s, exhibited a complexity of O(2nn2). More recently, a wide range of
algorithms with polynomial time complexity have been proposed. The most famous among
these is the Hungarian algorithm , developed by Kuhn in 1955 [19]. The time complexity
O(n4) of the original algorithm was later improved to O(n3) by Edmonds and Karp [12].
In this work, we use the auction algorithm to solve the linear assignment problem. The
algorithm was developed by Bertsekas in 1979 [2]. In our sett ing, it exhibits the same
time complexity as the Hungarian algorithm, namely O(n3). It is parallelizable and often
exhibits scalability, making it suitable for large-scale a ssignment problems. Furthermore,
it oﬀers a unique perspective on the optimization problem by simulating a bidding process
among the vertices to achieve an optimal assignment.
Because of the analogy to the auction setting, we call the ver tices from one set bidders
and the vertices from the other set items. Then, the naive auction algorithm operates in
successive bidding rounds. We denote by U the set of all unassigned bidders and by pi
the price of the item i, which is initialized to zero. The algorithm proceeds as fol lows:
(i) Pick any unassigned bidder i∈U and choose an item ji with the lowest cost, that
is,
ji∈ arg min
k=1,...,n
{d(i,k ) +pk}.

(ii) Assign bidder i to item ji. If item ji was previously assigned to another bidder k,
add k back to U.
(iii) Update the price of item ji to the level where bidderi is indiﬀerent betweenji and
the second best item, that is,
pji←pji +γi,
where
γi = min
j⁄=ji
{d(i,j ) +pj}− (d(i,ji) +pji).
(iv) If U is empty, terminate; otherwise go back to step ( i).
We called this process the naive auction algorithm as it is se riously ﬂawed. The bidding
increment γi can be zero if more than one item minimizes the cost. In this ca se, it can
happen that several bidders bid for a smaller number of items without raising their prices,
thereby creating a never-ending cycle. To solve this, we int roduce a positive scalar ǫ> 0
and change the updating rule of the prices to
pji←pji +γi +ǫ.
In other words, each bid must raise the price by a minimum posi tive increment ǫ. This
guarantees the convergence of the algorithm. The cost of the ﬁnal assignment diﬀers from
the optimal solution by no more than nǫ. For a formal proof of these two statements,
we refer the reader to Bertsekas’s paper [2]. As the distance s d(i,j ) are all integers, we
conclude that the assignment obtained upon termination is i ndeed optimal if
ǫ< 1
n.
It is noteworthy that the ﬁnal prices lie within an nǫ range of the optimal solution of the
dual problem. Therefore, the auction algorithm can be inter preted as a dual algorithm.
Using the auction algorithm, we implemented a Python progra m calculating the Lin-Lu-
Yau curvature and the 0-Ollivier-Ricci curvature of regula r graphs. The source code is
available in a public repository 1.

oldest in the ﬁeld of constructive combinatorics [29].

[25], and for d(n)∈o(√n) in 1991 [26]. The gap was closed by Liebenau and Wormald in
2017 [21]. Note that the complementary cases for d(n) larger than n/2 follow trivially.
For the asymptotic number of regular graphs up to isomorphis m, the study of the auto-
morphism groups of regular graphs is necessary. We refer the interested reader to [27] for
more details.
Although no closed formula exists, the number ofd-regular graphs withn vertices for small
values of n has been determined using algorithms designed to generate a ll regular graphs
with a speciﬁed degree and number of vertices up to isomorphism. In the following, we use
the algorithm GENREG, proposed by Meringer in [29]. It not only computes the numbe r
of regular graphs for the chosen parameters but also constru cts the desired graphs. Refer
to Table 1 for the number of connected regular graphs with a gi ven number of vertices n
and degree d, up to isomorphism, for n≤ 14.
6.3. Results. In this section, we present some of the results obtained by ap plying our
implementation of the Ollivier-Ricci curvature to the exha ustive lists of regular graphs
generated with GENREG.
The ﬁrst result concerns bone idle graphs.
Theorem 6.1. Let G = (V,E ) be a regular graph that satisﬁes |V| < 15. If G is bone
idle, then G is isomorphic to one of the following graphs:
(i) The cycle graph Cn for 6≤n< 15,
(ii) the bone idle graphs BIn for n∈{ 6, 7} deﬁned in Section 5.3.
We obtain this result by computing the Lin-Lu-Yau curvature and the 0-Ollivier-Ricci
curvature of all regular graphs with fewer than 15 vertices. Due to the rapidly increasing
number of regular graphs, this calculation becomes exceedingly complex for regular graphs
with more vertices.
The second result classiﬁes all regular graphs with Lin-Lu- Yau curvature equal to one.
Theorem 6.2. Assume G = (V,E ) is a locally ﬁnite, regular graph. Then Ric (G) = 1 if
and only if G is a cocktail party graph, meaning it is d-regular with d =|V|− 2.
For the proof of the theorem, we need the following Bonnet-Myers type theorem on graphs
by Lin, Lu, and Yau.

graph. If κ(x,y )≥k >0 for any edge x∼y, then the diameter of graph G is bounded as
follows:

The following theorem quantiﬁesMd for d equal to two and three.
Theorem 6.16. Let G = (V,E ) be a d-regular graph, satisfying Ric(G) > 0. If d = 2,

Theorem 6.17. Let G = (V,E ) be a 3-regular graph. Then κ0(x,y )≥ 0 for all edges
x∼ y if and only if G is a prism graph Yn for some n≥ 3 or a M¨ obius ladder Mn for
some n≥ 2.

prove Theorem 6.16.
Proof of Theorem 6.16. The only 2-regular, connected graphs are the cycle graphs Cn. It
is straightforward to verify that Ric(Cn) = 0 for n≥ 6. Hence, if G = (V,E ) is 2-regular
satisfying Ric(G)> 0, then G =Cn for some 3≤n≤ 5 and therefore|V|≤ 5 holds true.

Department of Mathematics, South China University of Techn ology, 381 Wushan Road,

Abstract. Let V be a strongly rational vertex operator algebra, and let g1, g2, g3 be
three commuting ﬁnitely ordered automorphisms of V such that g1g2 = g3 and gT
i = 1
for i = 1 , 2, 3 and T ∈ N. Suppose M 1 is a g1-twisted module. For any n, m ∈ 1
T N,
we construct an Ag3,n(V )-Ag2,m(V )-bimodule Ag3,g2,n,m(M 1) associated to the quadru-
ple (M 1, g1, g2, g3). Given an Ag2,m(V )-module U , an admissible g3-twisted module
M(M 1, U) is constructed. For the quadruple (V, 1, g, g) with some ﬁnitely ordered
g ∈ Aut(V ), Ag,g,n,m (V ) coincides with the Ag,n(V )-Ag,m(V )-bimodules Ag,n,m(V ) con-

T N, we show that the submodule of M(M 1, M 2(m)) generated by
the m-th component satisﬁes the universal property of the tensor product of M 1 and M 2.
Using this result, we obtain a twisted version of Frenkel-Zh u-Li’s fusion rules theorem.
1. Introduction
In the representation theory of vertex operator algebras, t he Zhu algebra [ Zhu96] and its
related bimodule theory [ FZ92] have played an important role. There are deep connections
between the representation of a vertex operator algebra and the corresponding associative
Zhu algebra. For example, there is a correspondence between the modules for a vertex
operator algebra and the modules for the corresponding Zhu a lgebra, and one can use
bimodules over the Zhu algebra to compute fusion rules of a ve rtex operator algebra, i.e.,
the so-called fusion rules theorem. There are many generali zations of the Zhu algebra A(V )
and its bimodule A(M ) theory. Dong, Li, and Mason generalized Zhu algebra theory i n two
directions. In one direction, for n ∈ N, they deﬁned a series of associative algebras An(V )
[DLM98c] with A0(V ) being identical to A(V ). They proved that a vertex operator algebra
V is rational if and only if An(V ) is semisimple for all n ∈ N. In the other direction, for
an automorphism g of V with ﬁnite order T , they deﬁned a twisted Zhu algebra Ag(V ) to
study the twisted representation theory of V [DLM98a]. They also deﬁned higher twisted
Zhu algebras Ag,n(V ) for n ∈ 1
T N later in [ DLM98b], and proved that V is g-rational if only
if Ag,n(V ) are semisimple for all n ∈ 1
T N. As for bimodule theory, Dong and Ren deﬁned a
series of An(V )-bimodules An(M ) for n ∈ N and proved a similar fusion rules theorem in
terms of these higher Zhu algebras and their bimodules. A spe cial case of twisted version
of bimodule theory was studied in [ JJ16], where for an untwisted module M and a ﬁnitely

A vertex operator module map YM (−, z), or more generally, an intertwining operator
I(−, z) among M 1, M2 and M 3, involves inﬁnitely many components, i.e., the coeﬃcients
of Y (a, z) or I(v, z) for a ∈ V, v ∈ M 1. The results mentioned above were built upon
the set of all weight-zero components. There are many more co mponents with nonzero
weight. Instead of just focusing on weight-zero components , considering all of the compo-
nents should give us more information about the representat ions of V . In [ DJ08b], Dong
and Jiang developed a more general bimodule theory. For m, n ∈ N, they constructed an
An(V )-Am(V )-bimodule An,m(V ) associated to V . Roughly speaking, An,m(V ) was built
upon the set of components with weight n − m generated by the vertex operator module
map YM (−, z). When n = m, the algebra An(V ) was recovered. Moreover, by putting
components with all possible weights together, they gave an other construction of the gen-
eralized Verma type module M (U ) generated by an Am(V )-module U , which was initially
constructed in [ DLM98b]. Later, in [ DJ08a], the authors generalized the An,m(V ) theory
to the Ag,n,m(V ) theory with A1,n,m(V ) = An,m(V ). This type of bimodule theory was
generalized to An,m(M ) for an untwisted module M in [ JZ19] by considering components
of intertwining operators I(−, z).
The ﬁrst goal of this paper is to develop a more general bimodu le theory over twisted
Zhu algebras. For each quadruple (M 1, g1, g2, g3), where g1, g2, g3 are three ﬁnitely ordered,
mutually commuting automorphisms of V satisfying gT
i = 1 for i = 1 , 2, 3 and g1g2 = g3,
and M 1 is a g1-twisted module, we are going to construct an Ag3,n(V )-Ag2,m(V )-bimodule
Ag3,g2,n,m(M 1) for n, m ∈ 1
T N. In this paper, we do this for a strongly rational vertex
operator algebra. Many known examples of vertex operator al gebras are strongly ratio-
nal, see Proposition 2.4. Under this assumption on V , any admissible g-twisted module
has a grading given by L(0)-spectrum. We show that the associative algebra Ag,g,n,n (V )
associated to the quadruple (V, 1, g, g) coincides with Ag,n(V ) constructed in [ DLM98b],
and the Ag,n(V )-Ag,m(V )-bimodule Ag,g,n,m(V ) associated to the quadruple (V, 1, g, g) co-
incides with Ag,n,m(V ) constructed in [ DJ08a]. For a quadruple (M 1, g1, g2, g3) and an
Ag2,m(V )-module U , we show that

is an admissible g3-twisted module. For the special quadruple (V, 1, g, g), we show that
M(V, U ) is the Verma type admissible g-twisted module M (U ).
One key step in constructing the Zhu algebra bimodule theory is determining the left
and right actions. Unlike [ DJ08b, DJ08a], where one product ∗g,n,m is enough to give both
left and right actions, in our case, we need to ﬁnd two, see ( 3.7) and ( 3.8).
The second goal of this paper is to give a twisted Frenkel-Zhu -Li’s fusion rules theorem.

Li gave the ﬁrst proof in [ Li99], and he pointed out that for this theorem to be true, some
conditions must be satisﬁed. Li then developed the regular r epresentation theory for vertex
operator algebras in [ Li02] and gave a more conceptual proof of the fusion rules theorem in
[Li01]. Another proof was given in [ Liu23] fulﬁlling Frenkel-Zhu’s argument. In the twisted
case, the corresponding twisted fusion rules theorem is sti ll open. We do this by ﬁrst
constructing the tensor product for two twisted modules in t erms of the bimodule theory
established in this paper. In the category of untwisted modu les, Huang and Lepowsky
developed a tensor product theory for vertex operator algeb ras in [ HL95a, HL95b, HL95c,
Hua95]. They proved that the module category for a vertex operator algebra V is a modular
tensor category under some convergence conditions of V . Li gave a construction of the
tensor product for two untwisted V -modules in [ Li98]. In his construction, Li used the
representation of the associated Lie algebra g(V ) of V . Li showed that the bottom level
of the tensor product M 1 ⊠ M 2 he constructed is A(M 1) ⊗A(V ) M 2(0). Using this result
together with the universal property of the tensor product, one can immediately prove
the fusion rules theorem. This inspires our bimodule approa ch in this paper. Suppose
g1, g2 are two commuting automorphisms of V with ﬁnite order, M 1 is an irreducible g1-
twisted module, and M 2 is an irreducible g2-twisted module. Let Tm(M 1, M2) be the

T Z-graded weight

a lowest weight module.
By Theorem 2.7, any irreducible g-twisted module M is a lowest weight module.

3. Bimodules over twisted Zhu algebras
For the rest of the paper, we assume V is a strongly rational vertex operator algebra.
By Proposition 2.4, V is g-regular for any ﬁnitely ordered automorphism g of V . Thus any
weak g-twisted module is a direct sum of irreducible g-twisted modules, and there are only
ﬁnitely many irreducible g-twisted modules up to isomorphism. For g ∈ Aut(V ), denote
the set of all irreducible g-twisted modules by Irr g(V ). Without loss of generality, we will
mostly deal with irreducible modules.

Remark 3.13. Our construction explains and recovers some known results:
• It explains, to some extent, why in [DLM96], to construct higher level Zhu algebras
An(V ) for n ∈ N, (L(−1) + L(0))a for a ∈ V was quotient out, while in the con-
struction of An(V )-bimodules An(M ) in [DR13], (L(−1) + L(0))v for v ∈ M was
not.
• When M 1 = V and g2 = g3 = g for some ﬁnitely ordered g ∈ Aut(V ), a series of
Ag,n(V )-Ag,m(V )-bimodule Ag,n,m(V ) was constructed for m, n ∈ 1
T N in [DJ08a].
The subspace Og,n,m(V ) deﬁned therein is contained in Og,g,n,m(V ). In particular,
when g = 1, it was proved in [Han22] that O1,1,n,m(V ) = O1,n,m(V ). We shall prove
Og,n,m(V ) = Og,g,n,m(V ) for any ﬁnitely ordered g ∈ Aut(V ) later.
Proposition 3.14. Let g ∈ Aut(V ) with ﬁnite order T . For any n ∈ 1
T N, the Ag,g,n,n (V )
associated to the quadruple (V, 1, g, g) is an associative algebra and it coincides with Ag,n(V ).
Proof. Og,n(V ) ⊆ O g,g,n,n (V ) by Proposition 3.10. Conversely, let M = L (Ag,n(V )), the
admissible g-twisted module generated by Ag,n(V ) as in Theorem 2.7, and take I = YM .

Then I ∈ I
(M

)
. Since V is g-rational, Ag,n(V ) is ﬁnite-dimensional, thus M is a g-
twisted module. Suppose a ∈ O g,g,n,n (V ), by Proposition 3.8, oM (a) |M (n)= oI
n,n(a) = 0 .
This implies [a] = [ a] ∗g,n [/BD ] = oM (a)[/BD ] = 0 , hence a ∈ Og,n(V ). Therefore Ag,g,n,n(V ) =
Ag,n(V ) as vector spaces. Moreover, by Remark 3.7, Ag,g,n,n(V ) = Ag,n(V ) as algebras. □
4. Properties of Ag3,g2,n,m(M 1)

Corollary 4.10. The admissible g-twisted module M(V, U ) coincides with M (U ). More-
over, Ag,g,n,m(V ) = Ag,n,m(V ) for any n, m ∈ 1
T N.
Proof. The ﬁrst part follows from Theorem 4.9 since both M(V, U ) and M (U ) satisfy
the same universal property in the category of weak g-twisted modules. For the second
part, note that Ag,g,n,m(V ) ⊗Ag,m(V ) U = Ag,n,m(V ) ⊗Ag,m(V ) U since they are both the
degree n piece of the generalized Verma type g-twisted module generated by U . Now take
U = Ag,m(V ), we get Ag,g,n,m(V ) = Ag,n,m(V ). □

Jet Modification and Medium Response - Theory Overview
Daniel Pablos1,∗
1Instituto Galego de Física de Altas Enerxías IGFAE, Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, E-
15782 Galicia-Spain
Abstract. This text contains a summary and personal perspective on the current
status and challenges of jet quenching physics as portrayed by the presentations
delivered at the 12th International Conference on Hard and Electromagnetic
Probes of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (Hard Probes 2024) which took place
in September 2024 in Nagasaki, Japan.
1 Introduction
Jets are collimated sprays of hadrons that are the result of the evolution in virtuality of en-
ergetic partons produced in hard scatterings. As they propagate through a deconfined QCD
medium, such as the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) formed in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC
and RHIC, many of their properties are heavily modified with respect to those measured in
proton-proton collisions. These set of phenomena, commonly referred to as jet quenching,
allow us to infer unique information about the QGP by means of model comparison to ex-
perimental data. The most prominent and well established of these modifications consist in
the depletion of high- pT jet yields [1], accompanied by an excess of soft particles around
the jet axis [2]. These observations are consistent with what one expects from energy loss
calculations due to the presence of deconfined QCD matter both at weak [3] and strong cou-
pling [4]. By energy-momentum conservation, it is expected that as the jet is modified by the
medium, the medium gets modified by its interaction with the jet as well. This backreaction
of the medium is known as medium response, and is mainly modelled using two di fferent
frameworks. For high-enough momentum transfers via elastic scatterings with the medium
constituents, one needs to consider the dynamics of the recoiling particles, which can further
reinteract with the medium. These physics probe the short-length, perturbative structure of
the QGP. For those lower momentum transfers of non-perturbative nature, or directly because
of the thermalization of softer jet partons, the excitation of hydrodynamic wakes is expected,
thereby probing the long wavelength features of the QGP.
A crucial step forward that has been undertaken in the last years has consisted in the ex-
tension of energy loss calculations from the static QGP brick setup to more realistic scenarios
where the dynamical nature of the medium is accounted for. Indeed, finding experimental ev-
idence of the spatiotemporal evolution of the flowing QGP using jet observables is one of
the key goals of jet quenching physics. In this conference we have witnessed exciting de-
velopments in this direction, such as new calculations on the e ffects of local medium flow
and gradients on stimulated gluon radiation [5–9] as well as predictions of drift effects caus-
ing jet deflection in preferred orientations [10–13]. Naturally, one also expects the evolution

arXiv:2504.21744v1  [hep-ph]  30 Apr 2025

===== PAGE 708 =====
