Remark 2.The lemma is motivated by the following observation. SinceL q1 ,→Lq0
forq 1 >q 0, controllings(λ,q)becomes more difficult asqincreases. This challenge
is particularly acute at the critical exponentq= 2n
n−2 due to the loss of compactness.
Therefore, if one has good estimates fors(λ 0,q 0), it is reasonable to expect they can
be transferred to obtain estimates fors(λ 1,q 1)whenq 1 <q 0 for a suitableλ 1.
From this viewpoint, the conditionq 1≤q 0 in (2.23) is essential, which is also
reflected in the proof. In deriving (2.25), the derivative was taken in the direction
of decreasingλ(equivalently, increasingq). Taking the derivative in the opposite
direction would yield a lower bound forE λ,q, which is not useful as we only possess
the upper bounds(λ,q)≤E λ,q(u).
Finally, we note that the inequality (2.23) is not sharp, at least for spheres.
For instance,[4]shows that onS n, the functions(λ,q)is minimized by constants
provided thatλ(q−2)≤n.

5.The Yamabe Constant forM×S 1(T)and The Yamabe Invariant
In this section we post a question on the Yamabe constant forM×S 1(T) for
arbitraryT >0, and some consequences on the Yamabe invariants ofS 2×S 2 if
this question has a positive answer.
5.1.Model.
The model we consider is from [23]: (S n−1×S 1(T), g0(T) =h std +dt 2), where
hstd denotes the standard round metric onSn−1 with scalar curvature (n−1)(n−2).
Letu T be a minimizer for the Yamabe constant of this manifold.
Via the covering map, the conformal metricu4/(n−2)
T gT lifts to a metric (u∗
T )4/(n−2)g∗
T
on the cylinderR×S n−1. BecauseR×S n−1 is conformally equivalent to (R n\
{0},dx 2), this lifted metric can be expressed asv
2n
n−2dx2 onR n\{0}, wherev
extends to a singular function at the origin.
By [7] the constant scalar curvature equation forcesvto be rotationally sym-

A Multi-Invariant Preserving Discrete Gradient Methods
Haodong Pu · Maohua Ran
Received: date / Accepted: date
Abstract This work introduces a novel structure-preserving methods for conservative systems
based on a predictor-corrector strategy. The framework applie s a discrete gradient correction
to predictions generated by explicit one-step or multi-step scheme s, which preserves nonlinear
invariants while maintaining the accuracy order of the original predic tor. This approach extends
naturally to problems requiring simultaneous conservation of multiple invariants. Under mild
conditions, conservation properties, solvability, numerical accur acy, and stability are established.
Long-term numerical simulations on Lotka-Volterra systems, sine -Gordon equations, rigid body
dynamics, and Kepler problems demonstrate improved robustness and conservation properties
compared to existing projection and relaxation methods.
Keywords Structure-preserving methods · Discrete gradient operators · Predictor-corrector
methods · Multi-invariant conservation · Numerical stability
Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation (2020) 65L05 · 65L06 · 65P10 · 65L20 · 65L70
1 Introduction
Structure-preserving numerical methods are designed to mainta in key geometric and physical
structures-such as symmetries, invariants, and symplecticity-in herent in diﬀerential equations.
Over the past few decades, signiﬁcant theoretical and computat ional advances have been made
in this ﬁeld. Among these developments, the preservation of invaria nts plays a particularly vital
role, as it is crucial for simulating long-term dynamics accurately in sc ientiﬁc and engineering
applications [20].
This work focuses on conservative systems of the form
{
y′(t) = f (y(t)), t ∈ [0,T ],
y(0) = y0, (1)

School of Mathematical Sciences, Sichuan Normal Universit y, Chengdu 610066, China
E-mail: maohuaran@163.com
Haodong Pu
School of Mathematical Sciences, Sichuan Normal Universit y, Chengdu 610066, China
E-mail: puhaodong10@163.com

2 Haodong Pu, Maohua Ran
where f : Rd → Rd is suﬃciently smooth, y0 ∈ Rd is the initial value. The system admits a ﬁrst
integralH(y) such that
H(y(t)) ≡H(y0), t ∈ [0,T ].
Consequently, the solution trajectory is conﬁned to the invariant manifold M = {y ∈ Rd |H(y) =
H(y0)}, a geometric constraint that structure-preserving numerical m ethods must respect by
ensuring the discrete solution yn satisﬁes H(yn) = H(y0).
Signiﬁcant progress has been made in structure-preserving nume rical methods, with Runge-
Kutta (RK) methods preserving arbitrary linear invariants [6] and s ymplectic RK methods con-
serving quadratic invariants, though no RK method can preserve c ubic or higher-degree poly-
nomial invariants [12]. This limitation has spurred the development of s pecialized algorithms,
including for Hamiltonian systems: variational integrators based on discrete variational prin-
ciples [18], Hamiltonian boundary value methods that exactly preserv e the Hamiltonian [3],
energy-momentum integrators for mechanical systems [23], and d iscrete Hamiltonian methods
using discrete directional derivatives [10]. Furthermore, techniqu es originally developed for gradi-
ent ﬂows-invariant energy quadratization [25] and scalar auxiliary v ariable approaches [22]-have
been extended to construct energy-preserving schemes for Ha miltonian systems [17, 8]. For gen-
eral invariants, widely used methods include the discrete gradient m ethod [19], Lagrange multi-
plier method [9], and projection method [11]; however, these typically require solving large-scale
equation systems with considerable computational costs, and the simultaneous preservation of
multiple invariants remains a fundamental challenge in the ﬁeld. To add ress this, eﬃcient strate-
gies such as the projected method [24] and the relaxed Runge-Kut ta (RRK) method [7, 15] have
been introduced, which reduce computational complexity by solving only one scalar equation
per time step. Despite these improvements, three practical challe nges remain in the design of
invariant-preserving integrators:
· Low-order accuracy : Classical discrete gradient methods are generally limited to ﬁrst- o r
second-order accuracy, since constructing higher-order discr ete gradients that simultaneously
satisfy the discrete chain rule presents substantial analytical diﬃ culties.
· Poor large-step robustness : Projection and relaxation-based methods (such as RRK)
exhibit robustness issues when the predictor direction is nearly ort hogonal to ∇H, or when
the time step exceeds stability limits.
· Non-modular multi-invariant conservation : Most existing methods are designed for
single invariants. For systems with multiple invariants, traditional pr ojection techniques re-
quire iterative projections or more intricate geometric treatment s, while multiple-relaxation
Runge-Kutta [1] and multiple-relaxation exponential Runge-Kutta methods [16] are inher-
ently constrained by their underlying Runge-Kutta or exponential Runge-Kutta frameworks.
Moreover, the existence of their relaxation parameters-and con sequently, of the numerical
solution-is guaranteed only under suﬃciently strict time-step rest rictions.
To overcome these limitations, this work introduces a discrete grad ient correction framework
with three core features:
· Compatibility: Enables decoupling of numerical accuracy from structure prese rvation, al-
lowing any explicit one-step or multi-step method to serve as predict or while maintaining
invariant conservation without order reduction through the corr ection procedure.
· Well-posedness: Theoretically establishes existence of the numerical solution for a rbitrary
time steps, while guaranteeing solution uniqueness under mild assump tions for suﬃciently
small steps.
· Scalability: The approach naturally generalizes to conserve multiple invariants simultane-
ously without modifying the core algorithmic structure.

analysis; Section 5 demonstrates eﬀectiveness through numerica l experiments; The conclusion
summarizes the main contributions.

Remark 1 When m = 0, the predictor (5) reduces to an explicit one-step method. This special
case ﬁnds frequent application in practical computations and will be demonstrated in subsequent
numerical examples.
Remark 2 Unlike standard projection methods, which are merely geometric po st-processing op-
erations, the DGC method preserves the structure of the under lying discrete conservation laws.
Since the correction equation (6) is implicit, we analyze the existence and uniqueness of its
solution. For a ﬁxed predictor yn+1, deﬁne the iteration function

4 Multi-Invariant Generalization
The DGC method can be naturally extended to conservative system s (1) possessing k invariants:
Hi(y(t)) ≡Hi(y0), i = 1, 2, · · ·,k, t ∈ [0,T ].
The corresponding DGC method for multiple invariant preservation is given by
{
yn+1 =φh(yn,yn−1, · · ·,yn−m),
yn+1 =g(yn+1,yn+1), (10)

i=1

Aλ = b. (11)
Here, A is the symmetric positive semi-deﬁnite matrix
A =

)
k×k,
and b is the vector

) ⊤
.
Theorem 4.1 (Existence) If all eigenvalues of the matrix A are positive and uniformly bounded
below by a positive constant C, then the DGC method (10) admits at least one solution.

Proof The continuity of the discrete gradient implies that A(yn+1,v ) is continuous in v. Given

b(yn+1)⊤A−1b(yn+1) ≤C−1‖b(yn+1)‖2.

that g(yn+1,v ∗) = v∗, which provides a solution to the DGC method (10). This completes th e
proof.
Theorem 4.2 (Consistency) Assume that all eigenvalues of the matrix A are positive and
uniformly bounded below by a positive constant C. If the prediction method φh has a local trunca-
tion error of order p, then the DGC method (10) also achieves a local truncation error of order
p.
Proof If φh has a local truncation error of order p, then
‖yn+1 −y(tn+1)‖ = O(hp+1), ‖b(yn+1)‖ = O(hp+1).
Consequently,
‖yn+1 −y(tn+1)‖ ≤ ‖yn+1 −y(tn+1)‖ + ‖g(yn+1,yn+1) −yn+1‖
≤ ‖yn+1 −y(tn+1)‖ +C−1/2‖b(yn+1)‖
= O(hp+1).
This establishes the desired result.
Theorem 4.3 (Conservation) The DGC method (10) preserves all invariants H1,H 2,...,H k
exactly, i.e., Hi(yn) = Hi(y0) for all n and i = 1,...,k .

Proof Taking the inner product of both sides of the correction scheme

Algorithm 1 outlines the DGC method (10) designed to preserve k invariants simultaneously,
with its applicability naturally extending to the single-invariant case (i.e ., k = 1).
Algorithm 1 DGC method (10) for preserving multiple invariants
1: for n = 0 to N − 1 do
2: yn+1 ⇐ φh(yn, yn−1, · · · , yn−m) // prediction step
3: yn+1 ⇐ yn+1 // initial guess
4: repeat
5: Compute A(yn+1, yn+1) and b(yn+1)
6: Solve λ ⇐ A−1b(yn+1)
7: Update yn+1 ⇐ g(yn+1, yn+1)
8: until
‖‖yn+1 − g(yn+1, yn+1)
‖‖ ≤ Tolerance
9: end for

Example 1 Consider the Lotka-Volterra model
{
y′
1 =y1(y2 − 2),
y′
2 =y2(1 −y1), (14)
which describes the population dynamics of a predator-prey syste m, where y1 andy2 denote the
populations of the predator and prey species, respectively. This m odel possesses a ﬁrst integral
H(y1,y 2) = lny1 −y1 + 2 lny2 −y2,
implying that the solution trajectories form closed curves.
We consider the initial value y0 = (2, 2)⊤ and integrate until T = 100. Model (14) is solved
using the following three methods:
· Standard forward Euler method.
· Projected forward Euler method.
· Discrete gradient correction method (DGC1), which combines the f orward Euler method with
the coordinate increment discrete gradient (4).
The numerical results are presented in Table 3, while the solution tra jectories and invariant
preservation are depicted in Figs. 1 and 2. We observe that:
· Under relatively large step sizes, the standard forward Euler meth od exhibits numerical in-
stability, while the DGC1 scheme maintains the theoretical converge nce order;
· At h = 2/3, Newton’s method used in the projected method shows high sensit ivity to the
initial guess, often leading to convergence failure. In contrast, a t the same step size, DGC1
preserves the invariant up to machine precision (see Fig. 2) and yield s the correct solution
trajectory;
· The update direction of the relaxed forward Euler method is tangen t to the invariant man-
ifold, resulting in the relaxation equation admitting only the trivial solu tion λ = 0. As a
consequence, the numerical solution remains ﬁxed at the initial sta teyn ≡y0 for all n, failing
to reproduce the true periodic dynamics.

6 Conclusion
The present work introduces the Discrete Gradient Correction (D GC) framework, a predictor-
corrector approach that converts arbitrary high-order explicit methods into invariant-preserving
integrators through an eﬃcient post-processing step. A centra l advantage over classical discrete
gradient methods is the elimination of the need to construct high-or der discrete gradients di-
rectly. The proposed framework demonstrates superior robust ness compared to projection and
relaxed Runge-Kutta methods under large time steps and can be na turally extended to preserve
multiple invariants via symmetric linear systems. Theoretical analyse s guarantee conservation,
order preservation, and stability under mild conditions, with numeric al experiments conﬁrming
long-term reliability. Application of the DGC method requires known inv ariant values at each
time step. In conservative systems, these values are determined by the initial conditions. Ex-
tension to dissipative systems, however, is not straightforward, as the corresponding quantities
are no longer conserved. Adapting the framework for such cases , potentially through estimation

===== PAGE 961 =====
18 Haodong Pu, Maohua Ran
of time-dependent targets or a reformulated correction proced ure, poses a challenge for future
research.

Generalized Frenet frames and frame sequences of singular space curves
Shun’ichi Honda
June 17, 2026
Abstract
The classical Frenet frame is defined by a concrete construction from the tangent, principal
normal, and binormal vectors of a regular space curve. However, this construction breaks down
at singular points and at points where the curvature vanishes. Motivated by this observation, we
reconsider the Frenet frame from an axiomatic viewpoint and identify the fundamental properties
that characterize it independently of its classical construction. Based on the theory of frontals
on the unit sphere and Legendre duality, we introduce a generalized Frenet frame for singular
space curves. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of a frame sequence, which gives rise to an
integer-indexed family of Frenet frames together with the corresponding curvatures and torsions.
This viewpoint provides a unified framework encompassing both the Frenet and Bishop frames of
space curves and the evolute–involute correspondence for spherical frontals. Moreover, explicit
recursive formulas are derived, revealing that the curvatures and torsions at each level encode,
respectively, the magnitude and rotational behavior of the invariants arising at the preceding level.
Keywords:generalized Frenet frame, frame sequence, higher-order curvature and torsion
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification.53A04, 53A55, 58K05
1 Introduction
The classical Frenet frame is one of the fundamental tools in the differential geometry of space curves.
For a regular curve with non-vanishing curvature, it provides an orthonormal frame consisting of
the tangent, principal normal, and binormal vectors, together with the curvature and torsion as a
complete system of invariants under Euclidean motions. However, the classical construction breaks
down at singular points and at points where the curvature vanishes. This observation suggests that
the classical construction may not fully reveal the essential geometric structure of the Frenet frame.
It is therefore natural to ask which geometric properties characterize the Frenet frame independently
of its classical construction.
In this paper, we reconsider the Frenet frame from an axiomatic viewpoint. Rather than starting
from the classical formulas, we focus on the geometric structure underlying the Frenet frame and
identify the fundamental properties that characterize it. This viewpoint leads naturally to the notion
of a generalized Frenet frame based on spherical frontals and Legendre duality. We prove that every
classical Frenet curve admits a generalized Frenet frame, while the definition also applies to a broad
class of singular curves. Furthermore, we introduce the notion of a frame sequence, which gives
rise to an integer-indexed hierarchy of Frenet frames together with the associated curvatures and
torsions of all orders. This framework provides a unified viewpoint on several classical constructions
in the differential geometry of curves. In particular, the classical Frenet frame and the Bishop frame
are recovered as the 0th-order and(−1)st-order Frenet frames, respectively. Moreover, the frame
sequence admits a natural interpretation in terms of the evolute-involute correspondence for spherical
frontals. We also derive explicit recursive formulas relating the curvatures and torsions at consecutive
levels. These formulas reveal that the curvatures and torsions at each level encode, respectively, the
magnitude and rotational behavior of the invariants arising at the preceding level.

for the associated curvatures and torsions.

If𝜃satisfies ⁄𝜃(𝑡)=ℓ(𝑡), then ℓ(𝑡)=0, and the frame{𝒃 1,𝒃 2,𝝁}is aBishop framealong𝜸.
We conclude with several remarks on the Bishop frame.
Remark2.13.The Bishop frame admits the following geometric characterization. Since ℓ(𝑡)=0, the
derivatives of𝒃 1 and𝒃 2 have no components along𝒃 1 or𝒃 2, and hence are always parallel to𝝁(𝑡).
Remark2.14.A Bishop frame{𝒃 1,𝒃 2,𝝁}obtained by rotation is not uniquely determined by the
original frame{𝝂 1,𝝂 2,𝝁}. Indeed, since𝜃is required only to satisfy ⁄𝜃(𝑡)=ℓ(𝑡), it is determined up
to a constant of integration.
3 Generalized Frenet frames
In this section, motivated by the geometric structure of the Frenet frame discussed in Remark 2.7, we
introduce a generalized Frenet frame for singular space curves.
Definition 3.1.Let𝜸:𝐼→R 3 be a smooth curve. We say that𝜸admits a (generalized)unit tangent
vectorif there exist a function𝛼:𝐼→Rand a map𝒕:𝐼→𝑆 2 such that⁄𝜸(𝑡)=𝛼(𝑡)𝒕(𝑡)for all𝑡∈𝐼.
In this case,𝛼is called the (signed)speedand𝒕the (generalized)unit tangent vector. Furthermore,
we say that𝜸admits a (generalized)Frenet frameif𝒕is a frontal in𝑆 2.
Suppose that𝜸admits a (generalized) Frenet frame. Let𝒕be a (generalized) unit tangent vector
of𝜸, and let𝛼be a corresponding (signed) speed. Since𝒕is a frontal in𝑆 2, we denote its dual
by𝒃:𝐼→𝑆 2. That is,(𝒕,𝒃)is a Legendre curve inΔ. We define𝒏(𝑡)=𝒕(𝑡)×𝒃(𝑡). Then
{𝒕(𝑡),𝒃(𝑡),𝒏(𝑡)}forms an orthonormal frame along𝜸. By Proposition 2.2, we obtain the following
corollary.
Corollary 3.2.Under the above notation, the following Frenet-Serret type formulas hold:

In view of the duality between𝒕and𝒃and the structure of the coefficient matrix in the Frenet-

Motivated by the above discussion, we call the frame{𝒕,𝒃,𝒏}constructed in this section a

Remark3.3.The case where the generalized unit tangent vector𝒕is regular was studied in [3].
Definition 3.1 may be regarded as an extension of that framework to the singular case.
The following examples illustrate the scope of the notion of generalized Frenet frames. We first
show that every classical Frenet curve admits a generalized Frenet frame, then construct one for a
singular curve, and finally present a regular curve that admits none.

generalized Frenet frame.

Remark4.3.For a Frenet curve, the 0th-order Frenet frame coincides with the classical Frenet frame.
On the other hand, the(−1)st-order Frenet frame corresponds to a Bishop frame.
Remark4.4.Similar higher-order invariants and hierarchies of invariants have appeared in the study
of ruled and developable surfaces, see [2, 5]. The main difference is that our approach focuses not
only on the invariants themselves but also on the recursive structure of the corresponding frames.
To better understand the recursive structure of the frame sequence, we consider the case where the
pair(𝜅 𝑘(𝑡),𝜏 𝑘(𝑡))does not vanish simultaneously. The following theorem gives recursive formulas
relating the𝑘th-order and(𝑘+1)st-order curvatures and torsions.

framed base curve and a spherical frontal, respectively. Hence the existence of a frame sequence is

A NON-CONVERGENCE PHENOMENON FOR THE
CR YAMABE FLOW
CLAUDIO AFELTRA, PAK TUNG HO, AND ANDREA PINAMONTI
Abstract.We construct a contact form on a three dimensional
CR manifold such that the CR Yamabe flow fails to converge. More
precisely, on small Rossi deformations of the standard CR three-
sphere, we exhibit an example whose corresponding CR Yamabe
flow develops a one-bubble concentration regime.
The construction is based on the negativity of the pseudoher-
mitian mass on the Rossi spheres. This shows that mass positivity
is not merely a technical assumption in the known convergence re-
sults for the CR Yamabe flow, but is genuinely connected to the
large-time dynamics of the flow.
1.Introduction
Given a compact Riemannian manifold (M,g), the Yamabe prob-
lem consists of proving the existence of a metric conformal togwith
constant scalar curvature. This problem, which has played a major
role in Geometric Analysis, has been solved through the works of Yam-
abe, Trudinger, Aubin (who settled the case of non-conformally flat
manifolds of dimensionn≥6) and Schoen (who settled the remaining
cases). The proof is based on the study of the Yamabe functional
R(g) =
R
MRgdVg
Volg(M)
n−2
n
,
whose critical points, when restricted to a conformal class, are solutions
of the Yamabe problem. The final step by Schoen requires the Positive
Mass Theorem.
Over the last few decades, flowing methods have attracted a consid-
erable attention in Geometric Analysis, and have been employed to try
to solve a lot of problems. The Yamabe problem is no exception, and
because of its variational form, it is quite natural to define a flow based
on it: indeed, up to an inessential renormalization, theL 2 gradient flow
of the functionalRis given by the following equation
∂g(t)
∂t =−(R g(t)−rg(t))g(t)
2000Mathematics Subject Classification.Primary 32V05, 32V20; Secondary
35R01, 53D10 .
1
arXiv:2606.27164v1  [math.DG]  25 Jun 2026

===== PAGE 977 =====
2 CLAUDIO AFELTRA, PAK TUNG HO, AND ANDREA PINAMONTI
wherer g(t) is the average scalar curvature ofg(t). It is easy to see that
if the Yamabe flow has a solution fort∈(0,∞) and ifg(t) converges to
some metricg∞, theng∞ is a solution of the Yamabe problem; therefore
it is natural to study whether global existence and convergence hold.
Both questions have been answered positively by Brendle: conver-
gence in low dimensions and long time existence in general in [B1], and
convergence in every dimension in [B2] (under the assumption that the
Positive Mass Theorem holds in any dimension).
These questions arise also naturally in the context of CR manifolds.
CR manifolds are defined as 2n+ 1-dimensional manifoldsMendowed
with a complexn-dimensional subbundleHofTM⊗Csuch that
[Γ(H),Γ(H)]⊆Γ(H) andH∩ H={0}. CR manifolds provide
an abstract model for real hypersurfaces in complex manifolds. They
are called nondegenerate ifH(M) =Re(H⊕ H) is a contact distri-
bution; in such a case the choice of a contact form determines a rich
geometric structure onM, in particular a metric onH(M) and a con-
nection. By contracting twice the curvature tensor of the connection
with the metric, analogously to Riemannian geometry, one gets a scalar
curvature invariant, called Webster curvature. Since a contact form is
determined up to multiplication by a nowhere-vanishing function, it is
natural to study the problem of finding a contact form such that the
Webster curvature is constant, known as CR Yamabe problem.
The CR Yamabe problem shows strong similarities with the Rie-
mannian one; in particular it is equivalent to finding critical points of
the CR Yamabe functional
Q(θ) =
R
MRθdVθ
Volθ(M)
(see Section 2 for the notation). In [JL], Jerison and Lee solved the
problem for CR manifolds of dimension 2n+1≥5 not locally equivalent
toS 2n+1 using a strategy analogous to Aubin’s in the Riemannian case,
while Gamara and Yacoub in [G, GY] settled the remaining cases; since
no analogue of the ADM mass was available at the time, they used
Bahri and Coron’s method of critical points at infinity, a topological
method based on the deformation of sublevels of the functionalQby
adding virtual critical points in order to bypass the failure of the Palais-
Smale condition. In particular they proved the existence of critical
points ofQ, but not of minimizers.
In [CMY1] Cheng, Malchiodi and Yang defined a notion of mass
for asymptotically flat CR manifolds (in dimension three, but easily
generalizable to higher dimensions as was done in subsequent works),
and proved a Positive Mass Theorem in dimension three, but with the
additional assumption that a certain fourth-order differential operator,
the CR Paneitz operatorP θ, is positive definite. They showed that the

===== PAGE 978 =====
A NON-CONVERGENCE PHENOMENON FOR THE CR YAMABE FLOW 3
pseudohermitian mass appears in the expansion of the Green function
of the conformal sublaplacian in a way similar to Riemannian geometry,
and as a result, they proved that ifPθ is positive definite, the functional
Qattains its minimum.
Later Takeuchi in [T] proved that the positivity ofP θ is equivalent
to embeddability inC N for someN, a condition that always holds in
dimensionn≥5 by a theorem of Boutet de Monvel (proved in [BdM],
see Theorem 12.2.1 in [CS] for a more recent exposition) but may fail
in dimension three.
In [CMY2] Cheng, Malchiodi and Yang estimated the pseudohermi-
tian mass of the Rossi spheresS 3
s, the simplest non-embeddable exam-
ple of a three-dimensional CR manifold (see Subsection 12.4 in [CS] for
a proof of this fact) and showed that it satisfiesm s =−18πs 2 +o(s 2),
and thus is negative for small values ofs. Using this result they showed
that on the Rossi spheres the CR Yamabe functional does not attain
its minimum, and therefore that in order to solve in general the CR
Yamabe problem, a non-minimizing proof like the one of Gamara and
Yacoub is required.
These results are not the only ones that show a breakdown of the
analogy between Riemannian and CR geometry which occurs only for
non-embeddable CR manifolds (and therefore only in dimension three):
in [AP] the first two named authors built a CR structure onS3 for which
the set of solutions to the CR Yamabe problem is not compact (un-
like Riemannian manifolds of dimension up to 24), and in [ACMY] the
first named author, Cheng, Malchiodi and Yang computed the vari-
ation (with respect to the CR structure) of the CR Einstein-Hilbert
functional onS 2n+1, observing that forn≥2 its behavior is essentially
the same as the analogous problem in Riemannian geometry, while on
S3 it behaves in the same way only on the subspace corresponding to
embeddable CR structures, and in the opposite way on the orthogonal
complement.
Motivated by the interest in the CR Yamabe problem, a flow analo-
gous to the Yamabe flow has been introduced in order to study it: the
so-called CR Yamabe flow is defined by

Since the Positive Mass Theorem fails for the pseudohermitian mass,
it is natural to ask whether convergence holds in general for the CR
Yamabe flow. In this article we answer this question negatively.

To our knowledge, this provides the first natural non-convergence ex-
ample for the CR Yamabe flow. Our construction shows that negative
pseudohermitian mass is not merely an obstruction to the convergence
of the flow; it gives rise to an instability of the flow itself, forcing the
solution toward a bubbling regime.
Let us describe the main idea behind the proof. The proof of conver-
gence uses a concentration-compactness principle to prove that, up to
subsequences, a non converging solution must blow up by forming bub-

NEW CONSTRUCTIONS RELATING REAL AND COMPLEX
CONTACT STRUCTURES
ALI M. ELGINDI
Abstract.We establish new connections between real and complex contact
geometry via embeddings of 3-manifolds intoC 3. We introduce a newcontact
wedgeconstruction combining two transverse real contact structures into a
complex one, subject to obstructions measured by the Nijenhuis tensor and
Dolbeault cohomology. Dually, we form ahedgeconstruction which extracts
real contact structures from complex ones. Applying these tools, we prove that
C3 admits uncountably many complex contact structures, using constructions
over the standard contactS 3 with Legendrian non-isotopic knots as complex
tangents.
MSC: 32V40, 57K33
Key words: contact structure, holomorphic
1.Introduction
We will make a relationship between real and complex contact structures in
the sense that we can construct new complex contact structures using a pair of
transverse real contact structures, in a process we call the ”contact wedge”. This
construction will be subject to the vanishing of two topological invariants.
Theorem 1.Let(ξ 1,ξ 2)be two transverse contact structures on a real 3-manifold
M. Then their wedgeδ=ξ 1∧ξ 2 defines an almost complex structure on a com-
plex 2-plane bundle, which extends to a complex contact structure in a neighbor-
hood ofMprovided the Nijenhuis tensor vanishes and the Dolbeault obstruction in
H 1(M,O(ξ 1⊗C))is trivial.
We will also formulate a new construction which we call the ”hedge” from which
we can construct a real contact structureξover a real 3-manifoldMwhich is itself a
submanifold of a complex manifoldNadmitting a given complex contact structure.
2.New Constructions
LetMbe a real closed, orientable 3-manifold. By the Explicit embedding the-
orem [3], there exists an embeddingF:M ,→C 3 such that the complex tangents
arise exactly alongγwith holomorphic tangent spaces beingξ| γ.
By our construction of the embeddingFabove, we have that the holomorphic
tangent bundle ofMisξ|γ, and we see thatξcan be extended as a real 2-plane
field over all ofC 3 which in turn can be considered as a holomorphic line bundle
as it inherits the complex structure over Stein. Furthermore, this holomorphic line
bundle can be assumed to be a (real) contact structure over real submanifolds (odd-
dimensional) ofM ,→C 3 andC 3 is Stein (see [4]). We then have a chosen vector

fieldv x given as the Reeb field of the contact structure overM, which gives an
induced trivialization for the tangent bundle ofMgiven as{v x,Jv x,nx}.
We designate a contact formαwith kerα=ξ. A 1-form defined overM⊂C 3
with complex tangents alongγcan be extended to all ofC 3 assuming the relevant
obstruction vanishes.
3.The Contact Wedge
In this section we determine the obstructions to the existence of a contact wedge
given a pair of transverse real contact structures on a real 3-manifoldM.
Theorem 2.Let(M,ξ 1,ξ 2)be a 3-manifold with two transverse contact structures.
Letγ⊂Mbe a knot. There exists an embeddingF:M ,→C 3 such thatγ
forms exactly the set of complex tangencies to the embeddingF. This embedding,
considered with the Fubini-Study metric, defines:
(1)A holomorphic line bundleηonF(γ),
(2)A real vector fieldρ(the Reeb field ofξ 2), normal toξ 1.
Given two transverse real contact structuresξ 1,ξ 2 onM⊂C 3, we need to ensure
their wedgeδ=ξ 1∧ξ2 is a complex contact structure on a neighborhood ofM⊂C 3.
We first define aC-linear operatorJonδ=ξ 1⊕ξ 2 such thatJ 2 =−I. By
transversality, at each pointx∈Mwe may writeT xM=ξ 1⊕L(x) whereL(x)
is a real line field, andξ 2 projects to containLisomorphically toξ 1. Stipulating
Jδ(v) =wforv∈ξ 1 as the unique vector inξ 2 corresponding tovmakesδinto an
almost complex structure.
The obstruction to integrability is given by the Newlander-Nirenberg theorem:
Jδ is integrable iff the Nijenhuis tensorN(J δ) vanishes.
Theorem 3(Obstruction for existence of the Wedge).The wedgeδ=ξ 1∧ξ 2 can
be given the structure of a complex contact structure on a neighborhood ofMinC 3
only if the almost complex structureJ δ is integrable. The primary obstruction is
the vanishing of the Nijenhuis tensorN(J δ)onM.
We assume the extension of holomorphic line fields overγextends naturally to
all ofMandC 3, which requires the vanishing of another obstruction given by sheaf
cohomology.
Theorem 4(Extension via Sheaf Cohomology).LetM⊂C 3 be compact. The ob-
struction to extending a holomorphic line bundle fromMtoC 3 lies inH 2(C3,M;Z).
SinceC 3 is Stein, this vanishes by Cartan’s Theorem B[1].

4.The Hedge
The hedge is the dual construction: extracting a real contact structure from a
complex one.
Definition 8(Hedge).Let(N,ψ)be a complex contact manifold of dimension
2n+ 1, and letξ⊂ψbe a holomorphic line subbundle. LetM⊂Nbe a totally real
submanifold of real dimension2n+ 1that is Legendrian with respect toIm(ψ). We
sayξis ahedgeofψoverMifξ| M is a real contact structure onM.
Theorem 9(Hedge Induces Contact Structure).Let(N,ψ)be a complex contact
manifold of dimension 3, andξ⊂ψa holomorphic line subbundle. LetM⊂Nbe
a totally real 3-manifold that is Legendrian with respect toIm(ψ). Thenξ| M is a
real contact structure onM.
Proof.Letθbe a holomorphic 1-form definingψ, soθ∧dθ̸= 0. Sinceξ⊂ψ= kerθ,
the formθvanishes onξ. RestrictθtoM. By the totally real condition,T pM∩
J(TpM) ={0}, so the real and imaginary parts ofθ| M are linearly independent.
Defineα= Re(θ| M). The Legendrian condition ensuresα∧dα̸= 0. Since kerα=
ξ|M by construction,ξ| M is a contact structure.□
Definition 10(Anti-hedge).Given a hedgeξ⊂ψ, theanti-hedgeis the holomor-
phic line bundleτdefined by the exact sequence:
0→ξ→ψ→τ→0.

Proposition 11(Anti-hedge is a contact structure).Let(N,ψ)be a complex con-
tact manifold of dimension 3, and letξ⊂ψbe a holomorphic line subbundle. Let
M⊂Nbe a totally real Legendrian 3-manifold with respect toIm(ψ). Ifξis a
hedge overM, then the anti-hedgeτ=ψ/ξrestricts to a real contact structure on
M, andξ| M⊕τ| M =ψ| M.
Proof.Letθbe a holomorphic 1-form definingψ, soθ∧dθ̸= 0. Sinceξ⊂ψ= kerθ,
the formθvanishes onξ. RestrictθtoM. By the totally real condition,T pM∩
J(TpM) ={0}, so the real and imaginary parts ofθ| M are linearly independent.
Defineα= Re(θ| M). Then kerα=ξ| M, and sinceMis Legendrian,α∧dα̸= 0.
Thusξ| M is a contact structure.
Now consider the quotientτ=ψ/ξ. OnM,τ| M is a real line bundle. The form
θvanishes onξ, so it induces a well-defined formθ τ onτby:
θτ([v]) =θ(v),
where [v] is the class ofv∈ψmoduloξ.
We claim thatτ| M is a contact structure. To see this, note thatθ∧dθ̸= 0 means
that the kernel ofθis a complex contact distribution. Sinceξ⊂kerθ, the formθ
descends to the quotientτ=ψ/ξ. Moreover, the conditionθ∧dθ̸= 0 implies that
the restriction ofdθtoτis non-degenerate: ifX∈τwere in the kernel ofdθ| τ,
thenθ∧dθwould vanish onξ⊕⟨X⟩, contradicting the contact condition.
Defineα τ = Re(θτ). Sinceθ τ is a complex-valued 1-form on the real 3-manifold

have:

5.Abundance of Complex Contact Structures
Theorem 12(Uncountability of Complex Contact Structures).The set of complex
contact structures onC 3 up to isotopy is uncountable.
Proof.We construct an uncountable family{ψ α}α∈I of complex contact structures
onC 3 that are pairwise non-isotopic.
Let (S 3,ξ std) be the standard contact 3-sphere. There exists an uncountable
family of Legendrian knots{L α}α∈I in (S 3,ξ std) that are smoothly isotopic but
Legendrian non-isotopic. For instance, one may take a family of torus knots whose
rotation numbersα∈R/Zare distinct. This is a standard result in Legendrian
knot theory [6].
Choose an overtwisted contact structureξ ot onS 3 that is transverse toξ std. Such
a pair exists because overtwisted structures are flexible and can be chosen to be

===== PAGE 997 =====
NEW CONSTRUCTIONS RELATING REAL AND COMPLEX CONTACT STRUCTURES 5
transverse to a given tight structure (see [4]). The space of contact structures onS 3
is large, and by the parametrich-principle for contact structures, we may assume
that the pair (ξ std,ξ ot) varies continuously with the parameterαwhen restricted
to appropriate neighborhoods of the knots.
For each Legendrian knotLα, we apply the corresponding explicit embedding as
by our theorem [3] to obtain an embedding
Fα :S 3 ,→C 3
such that the complex tangents ofF α are exactlyL α and the holomorphic tangent
planes alongL α areξ std|Lα.
The pair (ξ std,ξ ot) on the abstractS 3, together with the embeddingF α, defines
aformal complex contact structureδ α alongF α(S3) inC 3. Concretely, the wedge
constructionδ α =ξ std⊕Jξ ot gives an almost complex structure on a complex 2-
plane bundle overFα(S3). considering this bundle together with the almost complex
structure, will constitute a formal solution of the complex contact relation in the
sense of Forstneriˇ c [9]. The this formal construction varies continuously withα
because the embeddingsF α and the contact structures can be chosen continuously.
We now apply Forstneriˇ c’s parametrich-principle as given in Forstneriˇ c [9] which
provided for a parametrich-principle of complex contact structures on Stein man-
ifolds. Specifically, a continuous family of formal complex contact structures along
a closed totally real submanifoldM⊂X(whereXis Stein) can be deformed into a
family of genuine holomorphic complex contact structures on a Stein neighborhood
ofM, keeping the deformation fixed on a prescribed closed subset.
HereX=C 3 (Stein) andM=F α(S3) (totally real except alongL α). Applying
the parametrich-principle to the family{δ α}yields a family{ψ α}of genuine holo-
morphic complex contact structures defined on a Stein neighborhood ofF α(S3) in
C3. BecauseC 3 is Stein and contractible, eachψ α extends uniquely to all ofC 3.
Supposeψ α andψ β are isotopic as complex contact structures forα̸=β. Then
their formal data would be homotopic (by theh-principle), which would imply that
the Legendrian knotsL α andL β are Legendrian isotopic in (S 3,ξ std). However,
by constructionL α andL β have distinct rotation numbers and are therefore not
Legendrian isotopic. This contradiction shows that{ψ α}α∈I is an uncountable
family of pairwise non-isotopic complex contact structures onC 3.□
6.Conclusion
We have introduced two constructions relating real and complex contact struc-
tures. The contact wedge combines two transverse real contact structures into a
complex contact structure on a neighborhood inC 3, subject to vanishing of the
Nijenhuis tensor and a Dolbeault obstruction. The hedge extracts a real contact
structure from a complex one by restriction to a totally real Legendrian submani-
fold. As an application, we showed thatC 3 admits uncountably many non-isotopic
complex contact structures.

CATEGORICAL STRUCTURES OF KURANISHI SPACES WITH
L∞[1]-ALGEBRAS
TAESU KIM
Abstract.We introduceL ∞-Kuranishi spaces by associating, to each chart,
L∞[1]-algebras defined on open neighborhoods of points in the zero locus of
the Kuranishi section. We show that these objects collectively form a category
into which the category of smooth manifolds naturally embeds. Some notions
in [12] are modified to achieve the desired categorical structures; for instance,
the tangent bundle condition for chart embeddings is replaced by a quasi-
isomorphism condition for theL ∞[1]-structures.

1.Introduction
LetE→Ube a vector bundle over a smooth manifoldUwith a distinguished
smooth sections, and suppose that a finite group Γ acts on this data. For a compact
topological spaceX, we consider a Kuranishi chartU= (U,E,s,Γ,ψ) onX. This
means that each point inXadmits a neighborhood homeomorphic to the quotient
s−1(0)/Γ of the zero locus, as depicted in the following diagram:
E
X s−1(0) U.
π
ψ◦(·)/Γ,≃
Γ
s
Fukaya and Ono [11] introduced this notion to study the moduli space of
pseudoholomorphic maps in symplectic geometry. Their approach systematically
perturbs the sections, in a manner compatible with the Γ-action, to a transverse
one, ensuring thats−1(0) becomes a manifold. By patching together a chain model
ofs−1(0), they constructed a global object known as the virtual fundamental chain
ofX, which now serves as a foundation for Floer theory, Gromov-Witten theory,
and related fields.
Nonetheless, this approach has also revealed certain shortcomings. Most no-
tably, as remarked in [11], their method exhibits an undesirable dependence on
specific choices of the bundleEand the ambient spaceUof the zero locus ofs,
both of which should ideally be irrelevant.
To illustrate the issue more clearly, we begin with a simple example. Let
Vbe a finite-dimensional vector space. We consider the chart given byU×V:=
(U×V,E×V,s×id V,Γ,ψ).That is, the bundle is now given byE×V
π×idV
−−−−→U×V,
and the section iss×id V.The following immediate observation,
(s×id V )−1(0)≃s −1(0),
suggests that there should be a way to identify these two objects. Rather surpris-
ingly, no such identification exists yet; the notion of isomorphism of Kuranishi charts
in [12], defined by Fukaya-Oh-Ohta-Ono (abbreviated as FOOO), is too restrictive
to apply to this case.
The primary objective of this paper is to modify the theory of [11] and [12] in
order to minimize such dependencies, or, more precisely, to reformulate it within
a categorical framework where various choices can be handled coherently, thereby
rendering the ambient data trivial from the perspective of homotopy theory. To
achieve this, we incorporate locally definedL ∞[1]-algebras as the input for Kuran-
ishi charts, drawing inspiration from the notion ofL ∞-spaces discussed in [1], [2],
[4], [5], and [31].
Indeed, the incomparability ofUandU×Vin the above example, at both the
chart and space levels, is due to the lack of an appropriate notion of morphisms.
Our second goal is, therefore, to define morphisms of charts coherently up to those
of Kuranishi spaces. Consequently, we establish a category that naturally general-
izes the category of smooth manifolds. Within this framework, [19] shows that the
moduli space of pseudoholomorphic disks forms a well-defined object, assuming a
condition on the existence of certain stratification structures on the base manifolds
of the charts. Furthermore, this category is expected to exhibit additional favorable
properties from a homotopy-theoretic viewpoint, which is discussed in detail in [22].
Throughout this construction, we exploit the flexibility of the aforementioned
structures. By flexibility, we precisely mean the use of commutativity up to homo-
topy (instead of strict commutativity), which is typically satisfied with consider-
ably less effort. The definition ofL ∞-Kuranishi chart embedding is given partly in

terms of quasi-isomorphisms; accordingly, coordinate changes, as instances of such
embeddings, provide better opportunities to achieve our goal. In this process, the
homotopy invertibility guaranteed by the Whitehead theorem plays a crucial role.

1.4.Outline of the paper.The organization of this paper is as follows. In Section
2, we introduce the notion ofL∞-Kuranishi charts. Section 3 definesL∞-Kuranishi
spaces and establishes that they form a category with an appropriate notion of
morphisms. In Appendix A, we recall the theory ofL ∞[1]-homotopies and their
homotopies developed in [20]. Finally, Appendix B studies V-algebras, providing
the technical groundwork for the localL ∞[1]-structures that appear in the earlier
sections.

2.L ∞-Kuranishi charts
In this section, we propose a new chart-level theory for Kuranishi spaces. We
equip the base of each chart with a closed two-form, which induces a stratification
structure and a presymplectic neighborhood around each zero point. This additional
structure allows us to construct localL ∞[1]-algebras and a morphism between two
charts. Our notion of chart embedding generalizes the embedding of FOOO, in the
sense that their tangent bundle condition is reformulated as the quasi-isomorphism
of the correspondingL ∞-component.
2.1.Definition ofL ∞-Kuranishi charts.We present our definition of Kuranishi
charts, emphasizing the key differences from existing approaches.
Definition 2.1(L∞-Kuranishi charts).LetXbe a compact metrizable space. An
L∞-Kuranishi chartofXis given by a tuple
U= (U,E,s,Γ,ψ),
where
–U= (U,β) consists of a smooth manifold together with a closed two-form
β∈Z 2(U).
–π:E→Uis a (finite rank) vector bundle.
–s:U→Eis a smooth section.
– Γ is a finite group acting onUwhose action restricts to the zero set ofs,
i.e., Γ·s −1(0)⊂s −1(0).

Three points are worth noting here. First, the coordinate changes are required
to satisfy the compatibility conditionsonly on the zero locus.Second, the cocycle
condition is imposedon the base maps alone, and not on theL ∞[1]-component. The
reason for this is thatL ∞-compatibilities always hold (cf. Remark 3.2 (iii)); this
point is revisited in [21]. Third, we consider pairs (p,q) satisfying Imψp∩Imψq̸=∅,
whereas in the FOOO setting coordinate changes are defined only for pairs with
p∈Imψ q. Together, these three points yield the flexibility we seek to achieve.
FOOO Kuranishi charts, as defined in [12] and [13], can be regarded as special
cases of our construction in the following sense. Given an FOOO Kuranishi chart
U= (U,E,s,Γ,ψ), we equip its baseUwith the zero presymplectic formω U≡0.

3.The category ofL ∞-Kuranishi spaces
In this section, we introduce the notion ofL∞-Kuranishi spaces. An advantage
of working with thisL∞-version is that the set ofL∞-Kuranishi spaces forms a cat-
egory. In this regard, we define the morphisms between them, which are essentially
given by a collection of compatible chart morphisms.
3.1.L ∞-Kuranishi atlases.We can cover the underlying topological space with
L∞-Kuranishi charts, provided that they satisfy certain compatibility conditions.
Before presenting the definition of a Kuranishi space, we first introduce the notion
of anL ∞-Kuranishi atlas.Here, the termatlasshould not be confused with its
usage in other contexts in the literature, such as in [27].
Definition 3.1(L∞-Kuranishi atlases).LetXbe a compact metrizable space. We
say that bUis aKuranishi atlas onXif for eachp∈X,there exists a neighborhood
Vp ofpinX,a Kuranishi chart bUp = (Up,Ep,sp,Γp,ψp) andcontractibleU p for

Remark 3.2.(i) We adopt a convention Φ pq for the coordinate change (from

From now on and elsewhere in this paper, we always assume the strictness of
L∞[1]-algebras and their morphisms.
To define homotopies between twoL ∞[1]-morphisms, we need to introduce
the following notion:
Definition A.6(Models of ∆ 1×C).LetCbe anL ∞[1]-algebra. We say anL∞[1]-
algebraCis amodelof ∆ 1×Cif there existL ∞[1]-morphisms
Evalj :C→C, j= 0,1
and
Incl :C→C,
with the following properties:
(i) (Evalj)k≥2≡0, j= 0,1,Incl k≥2≡0.
(ii) Evalj, j= 0,1 and Incl are quasi-isomorphisms.
(iii) (Evalj)1◦Incl = idC.
(iv) (Eval 0)1⊕(Eval 1)1 :C→C⊕Cis surjective.
Using the notion of models, we can define homotopies betweenL∞[1]-morphisms:
Definition A.7(Homotopy).We say that twoL ∞[1]-morphismsf 0,f 1 : (C,{lk})→
(C′,{l′
k}) arehomotopicif there exist amodel of∆ 1×C′ denoted byC ′ and an
L∞[1]-morphismh:C→C ′ such that we havef j = Evalj◦h, j= 0,1.
Lemma A.8.[20, Lemma 3.3]Homotopies define an equivalence relation.
We introduce homotopy equivalences forL ∞[1]-algebras.
Definition A.9.AnL ∞[1]-morphismf:C→C ′ is ahomotopy equivalenceif
there exists anotherL ∞[1]-morphismg:C ′→Csuch thatg◦fandf◦gare
homotopic to idC and idC′,respectively.
Proposition A.10.[20, Proposition 3.7]Homotopy equivalences define an equiv-
alence relation.
We show that a key theorem on quasi-isomorphisms, which shows the useful-
ness of our definition.
Theorem A.11.Arbitrarily given two quasi-isomorphicL ∞[1]-morphismsf 0,f 1 :
C→C ′ are homotopic.
Proof.This theorem is a special case of [20, Corollary 4.6] for two morphisms.□
We close this section by stating anL ∞[1]-algebra version of the Whitehead
theorem over a field.
Theorem A.12(Whitehead theorem).[20, Theorem 3.13]Over a field and for
strictL∞[1]-algebras, a quasi-isomorphism is a homotopy equivalence.
